articles.title: Proposed city budget would add 3,535 staff positions by 2030, with transit asking for the most
articles.dek: The 2027-2030 budget before council would grow the City's workforce by 18.2 per cent, and councillors are split on whether that is needed growth or excess.
body: The City of Calgary's proposed 2027-2030 budget asks for 3,535 new full-time equivalent positions, an increase of 18.2 per cent that would take the workforce from 19,411 this year to 22,946 by 2030 [1].
Most of the growth would come early. The budget calls for 1,743 new positions next year, followed by 760 in 2028, 514 in 2029 and 518 in 2030 [1].

Calgary Transit made the largest request, at 648 positions, including bus and LRT operators and fleet mechanics [1]. The Calgary Police Service plans 524 new full-time positions by 2030, which includes 34 officers beyond the 275 it is able to hire next year, as well as 191 civilian roles [1].

Under the plan, City staff per 1,000 residents would rise from 12.26 to 13.58 by 2030. The budget document states that Calgary has fewer positions per resident than Toronto, Vancouver, Ottawa, Edmonton and Winnipeg [1]. Salaries, wages and benefits cost $2.7 billion in 2025, or 51.7 per cent of that year's operating budget, and the operating budget would pass $8 billion by 2030 [1]. The budget also requests $2.4 million a year from 2028 to lease more office space from third parties [1]. The proposal carries a 15 per cent property tax increase for 2027 [1].

Mayor Jeromy Farkas said police, fire and transit service cannot improve without more staff, but that some positions could be halted or delayed [1]. Ward 13 Coun. Dan McLean described the increase as bloat and said he sees room for savings in communications, human resources, information technology and supply management [1]. Ward 6 Coun. John Pantazopoulos said he is agnostic about the number of positions and is focused on outcomes [1].

Council's budget deliberations continue this week. The city clerk said public submissions would resume at 9:30 a.m. Wednesday, Nov. 25, with 218 speakers still registered after 98 people addressed council over the first two days [2]. Council has not yet voted on the staffing plan or the tax rate.

articles.title: School board says the city must secure high school land before the province will fund new schools
articles.dek: The Calgary Board of Education's chair told council during budget submissions that crowded high schools are waiting on land the City has not yet bought.
body: The chair of the Calgary Board of Education asked city council on Nov. 24 to find a lasting way to pay for high school sites, saying the province will not fund construction of new schools until the City has secured the land [1]. Board Chair Laura Hack spoke during public submissions on the City's 2027-2030 budget [1].

High school sites are bought with cash-in-lieu payments made to the City's Joint Use Reserve Fund, which go to the City's real estate department [1]. Hack told council that industrial levies were used for this in the past but are not sustainable [1]. The proposed capital budget includes $40 million for future land purchases for high schools and recreation centres [1].

The board's three-year school capital plan, approved last March, asks for 21 new schools. Three are senior high schools: Glacier Ridge and Livingston in year one, and Belmont/West Macleod in year two [1]. The province has not approved those projects [1]. City land purchase plans presented to the Infrastructure and Planning Committee on May 7 covered high school sites at Glacier Ridge, Keystone and Providence, of which only Glacier Ridge is on the board's priority list [1].

Space is tight. System-wide use of CBE buildings is about 95 per cent, against a target of 85 per cent, the highest in 10 years, and the 22 senior high schools average about 104 per cent [1]. Enrolment rose by more than 17,000 students between 2021 and 2024 [1]. Hack summed up the request in one line: "We need the high school land and space." [1]

The same day, the board's 2025-26 financial report showed a surplus of nearly $18 million [2]. Spending came in $21.5 million below plan, partly offset by $3.5 million less revenue, and enrolment was 3,739 students below forecast, which reduced provincial grants [2]. The board holds more than $7 billion in school buildings across 252 sites, and 60 per cent of its infrastructure is more than 50 years old [2].

articles.title: Recreation groups press council as 12 planned facilities go unfunded in the four-year capital plan
articles.dek: Speakers from sports groups lined up at the budget hearing while councillors floated ways to pay for more recreation space.
body: Recreation was the main theme of the second day of public submissions on the City's 2027-2030 budget, with advocates for motocross, ringette, basketball, hockey and cricket among those appealing to council [1]. A total of 98 speakers addressed council over the first two days [1].

The proposed capital plan funds several recreation projects, including $185 million to redevelop the Forest Lawn Aquatic and Fitness Centre, known as the Bob Bahan pool, $70 million for the Foothills Multisport Fieldhouse and $28.9 million for the Kingsland and Belmont athletic parks [1]. Twelve Wave 1 projects from the City's recreation plan, known as GamePlan, are not funded in the 2027-2030 capital plan, including an expansion of the Westside Recreation Centre [1].

Ward 2 Coun. Jennifer Wyness wants capital set aside for the long-idle fieldhouse moved to projects that are ready to build [1]. The chair of the fieldhouse society told council the province is considering the project for its 2027 budget [1].

Ward 6 Coun. John Pantazopoulos called the model of the City alone paying for $100-million to $200-million facilities broken and said he is considering amendments to increase recreation spending [1]. Ward 13 Coun. Dan McLean proposed paying for the Flourish Centre in Alpine Park with a split among the City, the province, Ottawa and fundraising [1]. Mayor Jeromy Farkas said projects the City would fund alone should be postponed until a willing partner is found [1].
Submissions were scheduled to resume Wednesday morning with 218 speakers still registered [1]. Council has made no decisions on the recreation projects.

articles.title: Two men charged after loaded handgun, $30,100 and suspected drugs found in northeast traffic stop
articles.dek: Police say officers on patrol stopped a car near Edmonton Trail N.E. on Tuesday morning after it missed a stop sign.
body: Two Calgary men face a combined 21 charges after police found a loaded handgun, cash and suspected drugs during a traffic stop in the northeast on Tuesday, Nov. 24 [1][2].

At about 10:30 a.m., District 3 officers on patrol saw two people inflating the tires of a heavily tinted white 2007 Audi A6 at a gas station in the 0-100 block of Fourth Street N.E. [1]. Police say the driver then missed a stop sign and failed to signal while turning onto Edmonton Trail N.E., and officers stopped the car on Marsh Road N.E. [1]. CTV News placed the stop in the Bridgeland area [2].

Officers said they smelled burning cannabis and detained both men under the Gaming, Liquor and Cannabis Act [1]. Police say the driver resisted arrest, and the passenger was arrested after officers saw drug paraphernalia [1].

Police say they seized suspected methamphetamine and fentanyl, drug paraphernalia, a scale, $30,100 in cash and a loaded Canik 9 mm handgun with a 15-round magazine [1]. No drug quantities were released [1].

A 56-year-old Calgary man faces eight charges, including careless storage of a firearm, carrying a concealed weapon, possessing property obtained by crime over $5,000 and obstructing a police officer [1]. A 43-year-old Calgary man faces 13 charges, including firearm storage and weapons offences and five counts each of possessing a weapon and possessing ammunition while under a prohibition order [1]. Both are due in court on Thursday, Nov. 26 [1]. The charges have not been proven in court.
Acting Staff Sgt. Shona Brunton of District 3 said in the release that a loaded firearm is "especially concerning" [1]. Police ask anyone with information to call 403-266-1234 [1].

articles.title: Water use stays under 500 million litres for another two days as Stage 4 rules continue
articles.dek: Calgary used 489 million litres on Monday and 491 million on Tuesday, keeping the city in the green zone while the Bearspaw feeder main is connected.
body: Calgary's water use stayed below the City's daily target again early this week, with 489 million litres used on Monday, Nov. 23, and 491 million litres on Tuesday, Nov. 24 [1][2]. Stage 4 outdoor water restrictions remain in effect [2][3].

The City asks residents to keep demand below 500 million litres a day while crews connect the new Bearspaw south feeder main, which keeps the city in what it calls the green zone [1][3]. The City's restrictions page, updated Nov. 24, thanked residents for keeping the streak alive but did not give a count of days under the limit [1].

The shutdown of the existing main was expected to last about four weeks from Nov. 4 [1]. The City says no restrictions are expected while the new main is commissioned in December [1]. The most recent estimate reported for lifting the current restrictions is early December [4]. The City has not announced a firm end date.
Use has been steady over the past several days. Calgary used 476 million litres on Saturday, Nov. 21, and 490 million litres on Sunday, Nov. 22 [4].
Residents can follow the daily figures and the rules in effect on the City's water restrictions page [1].

articles.title: Chinook brings a mild end to the work week before temperatures fall below zero
articles.dek: Highs near 9 C are forecast for Thursday, with a cooldown to below-freezing highs by Monday.
body: An overnight chinook gave Calgary a warm start on Wednesday, and temperatures are expected to stay above seasonal for the rest of the work week [2]. Environment Canada recorded 9.9 C at Calgary International Airport at 5 p.m. Wednesday under mostly cloudy skies, and no weather alerts were in effect [1].

The forecast calls for south winds of 20 km/h gusting to 40 on Wednesday night, with a low of -1 C [1]. Thursday is expected to be mainly cloudy with a high of 9 C and west winds of 30 km/h gusting to 50 in the afternoon [1].

Friday and Saturday are forecast to be sunny, with highs of 8 C and 4 C [1]. Temperatures then drop, with a high of 1 C on Sunday, -3 C on Monday and -1 C on Tuesday, Dec. 1, under a mix of sun and cloud [1]. Overnight lows are forecast at 1 C on Thursday night and 0 C on Friday night, then -4 C on Saturday night, -7 C on Sunday night and -9 C on Monday night [1].
The forecast lists no precipitation amounts for the coming days [1]. The mild spell comes as outdoor water restrictions remain in place across the city.

articles.title: Alberta plans Sovereignty Act motion against the federal Combatting Hate Act
articles.dek: The province says the federal law's removal of a good-faith religious opinion defence creates uncertainty, and wants cabinet to consider lawful steps in response.
body: The Alberta government says it will bring a motion under the Alberta Sovereignty within a United Canada Act in response to the federal Combatting Hate Act [1]. The motion must be passed by the legislature, and the government's announcement on Nov. 24 did not give it a number [1].

According to the province, the federal act removes a Criminal Code defence for people who express religious beliefs or opinions in good faith [1]. The motion would affirm fundamental freedoms and urge cabinet to consider lawful steps to protect Albertans from the federal law [1].

The steps the province proposes include protecting lawful political and religious expression, keeping people able to read and quote sacred texts, educating Albertans about their rights and continuing to address crime [1]. The announcement also points to the Alberta Bill of Rights, the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the Criminal Code [1].

The announcement was made by Premier Danielle Smith and Mickey Amery, Minister of Justice and Attorney General [1]. Amery said removing the good-faith religious opinion defence "creates unnecessary uncertainty for Albertans" [1].

The province noted earlier steps. In August, the public safety minister told police that stopping crime, not policing opinions, is the priority, and in September the Attorney General directed the Alberta Crown Prosecution Service to give significant weight to freedom of expression [1]. The Attorney General's consent is still required before certain hate-related charges can proceed [1]. The federal government's response was not included in the provincial announcement.

articles.title: Alberta eases school flag rules so existing schools do not need new outdoor poles
articles.dek: From Jan. 4, schools will display the Canadian and Alberta flags based on how many outdoor poles they already have.
body: The Alberta government has changed its school flag rules so existing schools will not need to install new outdoor flagpoles [1]. The amendment to the Flag Display Regulation takes effect on Jan. 4, 2027 [1].
The change reverses an earlier plan that required both the Canadian and Alberta flags to fly outdoors on separate poles, and the province says it responds to feedback from school boards [1].

Under the new rule, a school with no outdoor pole will display both flags indoors [1]. A school with one outdoor pole will fly the Canadian flag outside and display the Alberta flag prominently inside [1]. A school with two poles will fly both flags outdoors [1]. The Canadian flag takes priority, and each pole carries one flag [1].
New schools will be built with two outdoor flagpoles, so both flags can fly outside at those buildings [1].

The announcement was made by Demetrios Nicolaides, Minister of Education and Childcare, who said the flags "deserve a place of pride in schools across Alberta" [1]. The rule applies to schools across the province, including those run by Calgary's public and Catholic boards.

articles.title: Flames drop 2-1 decision in Ottawa and visit Pittsburgh on Wednesday night
articles.dek: Calgary outshot the Senators but fell behind early, and now sits at 10-13-2 heading into a road game against the Penguins.
body: The Calgary Flames lost 2-1 to the Ottawa Senators on Monday, Nov. 23, at Canadian Tire Centre [1]. Ottawa scored twice in the first period, through Michael Amadio at 12:16 and Shane Pinto at 17:36 [1]. Matt Coronato scored Calgary's goal on the power play at 15:40 of the third period [1].

Ottawa goaltender Linus Ullmark made 35 saves, and Devin Cooley made 29 for Calgary [1]. Head coach Ryan Huska said after the game that he did not like how his team started [1]. Forward Joel Farabee also pointed to a flat start [1]. The loss left the Flames with a record of 10-13-2 [1].

The Flames visit the Pittsburgh Penguins on Wednesday, Nov. 25, at 5 p.m. Calgary time at PPG Paints Arena [2]. Pittsburgh is 8-6-4 in its last 18 games against Calgary [2]. Before the game, the Flames had 22 points and a 4-7-1 road record, while the Penguins were 7-14-2 with 16 points [3].
In goal this season, Cooley is 5-6-0 with a .909 save percentage and Dustin Wolf is 5-6-2 with a .877 save percentage [3]. The result of Wednesday's game was not available at publication time.

articles.title: Police request comes under scrutiny as council moves into budget questions, with housing a theme at the hearing
articles.dek: The mayor called the Calgary Police Service's capital request unprecedented as council worked through the proposed 2027-2030 budget, while many speakers at the public hearing pointed to housing.
body: Calgary city council is working through the proposed 2027-2030 budget this week, after a public hearing that began on Monday, Nov. 23, and with questions for City staff set for Tuesday [3]. Nothing has been decided yet [3]. The proposal calls for a 15 per cent property tax increase next year [1][2].

The Calgary Police Service's request has become one of the most closely watched items. The proposed budget includes more than $3 billion for police operations and new capital, which a CBC photo caption puts at $3.3 billion over four years, enough for more than 300 new officers and more than 200 new civilian employees [1]. Mayor Jeromy Farkas called the police capital request unprecedented and said a 73 per cent increase cannot go ahead without some areas being optimized or deferred [1]. He described the police budget as a significant contributor to the proposed tax increase [1].

Calgary Police Commission chair Amtul Siddiqui described it as a catch-up budget after earlier cycles that she said did not provide enough, and said the commission had already cut the request as far as it could [1]. She said similar growth requests are likely in the next couple of budget cycles as the city's population nears two million [1]. A police commission report found the service had spent 46 per cent of its capital budget by July, which the City called historically low; Siddiqui said part of that was due to delays in buying land for a southeast district office in Belvedere and an indoor firearms range [1].

Ward 2 Coun. Jennifer Wyness, who previously sat on the police commission, said the service is not immune from efficiency pressures and that she is considering a budget amendment to change the police funding amount [1]. The budget also redirects $28 million from city reserves to cover a shortfall after the province limited photo radar revenue, and includes $27 million for more transit safety officers, $8 million for community standards peace officers and $4.5 million for traffic safety officers [1].

At Monday's hearing, the speaker list started at 249 people and grew past 260, each with five minutes [2]. Housing came up repeatedly, with speakers linking it to social disorder tied to mental health and addiction [2]. Chris Bell, chief executive of Norfolk Housing, told council that 15 per cent of Calgary households are in core housing need, and that more non-market housing would ease pressure on city services [2]. Calgary Police Association president John Orr supported the police request but said, "funding alone will not solve the crisis we are facing" [2].

Ward 7 Coun. Myke Atkinson asked how council could avoid another large police increase in four years, pointing to work on root causes such as housing [2]. After the hearing, councillors move to questions of administration and then to amendments, 69 of which were on the list at last count [2]. Meetings start at 9:30 a.m. each day and, starting Tuesday, end at 6 p.m. [2].

articles.title: Woman dies after fire in Kingsland apartment building, one of three fires overnight
articles.dek: Firefighters found a woman unconscious in a smoke-filled suite on Elbow Drive S.W.; two other fires in Rosscarrock and Taradale caused no injuries.
body: A woman died after a fire in a three-storey apartment building in southwest Calgary on Monday night, Nov. 23 [1][2][3]. The Calgary Fire Department was called at about 9:45 p.m. to the 7700 block of Elbow Drive S.W., a 12-unit building in the Kingsland neighbourhood just south of Henry Wise Wood High School [1][3].

When crews arrived, residents were already getting out, and heavy smoke and fire were coming from a third-floor window [1][2]. Firefighters began with hose lines from outside, then moved inside to put out the fire while searching the building and helping people leave [1]. Two people had smoke inhalation, and a cat was found dead in the suite where the fire was burning [1][3].

In the next apartment, crews met what the fire department described as blackout smoke conditions and found a woman unconscious [1]. She was carried outside, where firefighters and EMS paramedics tried to revive her, and she was pronounced dead on the way to hospital [1][2][3]. Crews stayed at the scene through the night to support investigators and keep the site safe [1].

Firefighters responded to two more structure fires before the night was out [1][3]. At 11:10 p.m., a garage caught fire in the 1400 block of 39 Street S.W., in the Rosscarrock area; the fire stayed in the garage and no one was hurt [1][3]. At 12:25 a.m. on Tuesday, crews went to a multi-family home in the northeast community of Taradale, where smoke was coming from the front door and the occupants had already left [1]. Firefighters put out a kitchen fire and checked for hot spots, and no injuries were reported [1][3].

The causes of all three fires are under investigation and have not been determined [1][2][3]. The City used the incidents to remind residents to make sure smoke alarms are installed, tested and working, and Global News reported the reminder also covered carbon monoxide detectors [1][3]. One early report placed the Elbow Drive fire in the southeast, but the address given by the fire department is in the southwest [1][2].

articles.title: Alberta bill would end automatic public inquiries into deaths in custody and raise voter-data fines to $1 million
articles.dek: Bill 44, an omnibus justice and public safety bill tabled Monday, changes 20 provincial laws, from fatality inquiries and voter lists to roadside breath tests and the sheriffs' police service.
body: The Alberta government tabled Bill 44, the Justice, Public Safety and Information Statutes Amendment Act, 2026, on Monday, Nov. 23 [1][2][3]. The omnibus bill, which received first reading that afternoon, amends 20 provincial laws [3]. Justice Minister Mickey Amery and Public Safety and Emergency Services Minister Mike Ellis announced it at a news conference [2][3].

Today, a public fatality inquiry is mandatory when someone dies in jail or in police custody, unless the death was not preventable or was from natural causes [1]. The bill would replace that with an assessment, give medical examiners more power to investigate deaths instead, and leave the justice minister able to order an inquiry [1][3]. Under the change, the Fatality Review Board would recommend an inquiry when it decides one is in the public interest [4]. Alberta has 180 public inquiries waiting to be heard, 125 of them mandatory and 55 discretionary, and some take 8 to 14 years [3]. Neither the bill nor the news conference said what would happen to the 125 pending mandatory inquiries [3]. Amery said, "We can't allow families to be waiting years" [1].

The bill also sets permanent rules for who can get Alberta's list of electors, after names and addresses were posted in a searchable online database earlier this year [1][2]. Wilfully breaking those rules would become a corrupt practice punishable by fines of up to $1 million, up to two years in jail or both, compared with a current maximum of $100,000 and one year [3]. Parties would need a $100,000 refundable deposit for province-wide access, and candidates and MLAs a $2,000 deposit [3]. Amery said the higher penalties would not apply to the earlier breach, citing legal advice against retroactive penalties [3].

Other changes would make the Alberta Sheriffs Police Service part of government, replace roadside appeals with two breath samples taken at least 15 minutes apart, and let a provincial statistics office receive identifiable health information without consent for approved data projects, with reports de-identified [2][3]. Several parts take effect only when proclaimed [3].

Alberta NDP justice critic Irfan Sabir said the government cannot be trusted to protect information, pointing to the earlier voter list breach [2]. NDP public safety critic David Shepherd said the bill advances a provincial sheriff police service without public consultation [2].

articles.title: City memo flags risks to CTrain projects and bike lanes from Alberta's Bill 43
articles.dek: A memo to council says the provincial roads bill would add approval steps and leave Calgary carrying much of the cost and delivery risk.
body: An internal City of Calgary memo warns that Alberta's Bill 43 could bring longer approval timelines and unbudgeted costs for major transit and bike lane projects, LiveWire Calgary reported on Tuesday, Nov. 24 [1]. The City's government relations team sent the memo to councillors and the executive leadership team on Nov. 20 [1].

Bill 43, the Transportation (Safe and Sensible Roads) Statutes Amendment Act, was tabled in the legislature the week before [1]. According to the memo, the bill increases provincial control over major transportation projects while leaving the City responsible for much of the cost of carrying them out and the risk of delivering them [1].

The memo lists four main risks: longer and less predictable approval timelines; exposure to redesign or removal of planned and existing assets; possible unbudgeted costs to comply or restore; and less municipal control [1]. It rates urban rail transit as high risk for timelines, liability and cost, citing possible ministerial changes to projects, financial liability for changes outside the City's control, and effects on design, cost escalation and money already spent [1]. Kelly Cote, the City's manager of government relations, wrote, "Additional provincial approval dependencies would reduce schedule certainty" [1].

For bike lanes, the memo says provincial approval could become part of road renewal projects that include them, creating uncertainty about the network over its lifespan [1]. It also cites the cost of tearing lanes out and the chance that existing bike infrastructure could be left stranded if parts are removed or changed [1]. The memo, as reported, does not put a dollar figure on these risks [1].

Asked on Tuesday about the rail concerns, the Ministry of Transportation and Economic Corridors repeated a statement from last week attributed to Minister Devin Dreeshen, saying the province will work with municipalities to limit future bike lanes in high-traffic areas and deal with existing problem lanes [1]. Mayor Jeromy Farkas said last week he was concerned about provincial micromanagement of multi-billion-dollar transit projects, pointing to the Green Line, and said the premier's office had told him the City will not pay for future bike lane removals [1]. The bill has not passed, and Premier Danielle Smith has said amendments could be coming [1].

articles.title: WinSport cleared to use water for overnight snowmaking as feeder main work stays on schedule
articles.dek: Calgary used 489 million litres on Monday, below the 500-million-litre target, and the City has given WinSport a limited exemption of up to 3 million litres a night.
body: The City of Calgary has given WinSport a limited exemption from Stage 4 water restrictions, allowing it to use up to 3 million litres of water a night for snowmaking when the weather allows [1][2]. The City can withdraw the permission at any time [2]. WinSport made only a small amount of snow overnight, and the City said the forecast leaves no chance to make more over the next few days [1].

Even after restrictions lift, WinSport will be held to about 40 per cent of its snowmaking capacity until the new Bearspaw South Feeder Main is fully in service, which the City expects in mid-to-late December [1][2]. Calgary Citizen reported the limit stems from changes made after last year's feeder main break [2].

Water use stayed under the daily target of 500 million litres, which covers Calgary and neighbouring communities [1]. Demand was 489 million litres on Monday, Nov. 23 [1][3]. Calgary Citizen reported 476 million litres on Saturday and 490 million on Sunday [2]. Restrictions began on Nov. 4 and remain on track to end in early December [2].

Work to connect the new feeder main is in its third week and on schedule at every site, the City said [1][2]. At the Shaganappi Pump Station, the new pipe has been connected and inspected and is ready to receive water [1]. At 89 Street and 33 Avenue N.W., crews working around the clock have placed and connected a new steel T-joint linking the new main to the existing pipe from the Bearspaw Water Treatment Plant, and welding continues [1][2]. At 83 Street and 33 Avenue N.W., extra work on an existing pipe meant a wider dig, but the job is still on schedule, with overnight backfilling planned later this week [1][2].

Pipe installation is complete at all five locations near Parkdale Boulevard and Memorial Drive N.W., where crews are backfilling and repairing the surface, and the City said recommissioning of those pipes was expected to begin the next day [1]. A City statement said, "Protecting our water supply remains our top priority" [1].

articles.title: Man faces 22 charges after police say he kept driving stolen and seized vehicles while under release orders
articles.dek: The Calgary Police Service auto theft team recovered a stolen Toyota Land Cruiser and seized a Maserati after an arrest in southeast Calgary.
body: A Calgary man faces 22 charges after police say he was repeatedly seen driving while release orders barred him from doing so, the Calgary Police Service said on Monday, Nov. 23 [1][2]. The service's auto theft team said he was seen behind the wheel numerous times between Thursday, Oct. 15, and Friday, Nov. 6 [1].

Police said the vehicles included a stolen Toyota Land Cruiser and a Maserati [1][2]. The Maserati was not stolen, but driving any vehicle was a breach of his release conditions, police said [1]. Officers recovered the vehicles and seized the Maserati for further investigation, and also recovered property belonging to victims and items they believe are linked to vehicle theft [1].

The man was arrested on Friday, Nov. 6, outside a home in the 2600 block of 43 Street S.E. [1]. He is charged with one count of theft of a motor vehicle, three counts of driving while prohibited, one count of possessing break-and-enter instruments, one count of driving without insurance and eight counts of breaching a release order [1]. Police also executed eight outstanding warrants, bringing the total to 22 [1].

His next court appearance is set for Friday, Nov. 27 [1]. None of the charges has been proven in court. Police said the investigation is continuing and asked anyone with information to call the non-emergency line at 403-266-1234 [1].

articles.title: SAIT's Highwood restaurant reopens as new spots open downtown and in Marda Loop and Rosso closes a café
articles.dek: The student-run Highwood is back in a renovated space in the John Ware Building, while Rosso Coffee Roasters is closing its 17 Avenue S.E. café on Nov. 27.
body: The Highwood Kitchen + Bar, the restaurant run by SAIT students, reopened in its renovated home in the John Ware Building on Friday, Nov. 20, Calgary Citizen reported [1]. The restaurant has 230 seats, and its new bar also serves as a classroom for SAIT beverage students [1]. SAIT's website lists the restaurant's menu [2].

Several other restaurants have opened in recent weeks [1]. Alva, from the group behind Murrieta's, is now open on the ground floor of The Edison at 9 Avenue and 1 Street S.W., with a menu built around Canadian ingredients [1]. In Marda Loop, Saint Vincent, a neighbourhood steakhouse from the original founders of Una Pizza + Wine, serves Spanish-inspired plates for sharing [1]. Sushi Jun, an eight-seat omakase counter, was ranked second on Air Canada's list of the country's best new restaurants for 2026, behind only Restaurant Capelin in St. Catharines, Ont. [1].

Rosso Coffee Roasters is closing its 17 Avenue S.E. café for good as of Nov. 27 [1]. The company's Coats for Coffee drive continues to Dec. 15 at four other locations: Ramsay, Stephen Avenue, Inglewood and Tuxedo [1]. People who bring a clean, gently used winter coat or accessory for the Project Warmth Society of Alberta receive a coffee in return [1].

Holiday pop-ups are also back. Proof's Christmas cocktail bar runs until Dec. 24, open daily from 2 p.m. to 1 a.m. with no reservations, and Tops Pizza South has become a holiday lounge until Dec. 23 [1]. At CORE Shopping Centre, a Black Friday promotion starting Wednesday adds a $25 bonus card to $250 gift card purchases, with a limit of two per person [1].

articles.title: Three Calgary police officers charged with manslaughter in 2024 death of man at southeast hotel
articles.dek: Alberta's police watchdog says three constables face manslaughter and assault charges in the death of a 42-year-old Blood Tribe man after a call to a Macleod Trail hotel.
body: Three Calgary Police Service officers have been charged with manslaughter in the September 2024 death of a 42-year-old Blood Tribe man, Alberta's police watchdog announced on Monday, Nov. 23 [1][2][3].

The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) said Const. Roy Braun, Const. Filip Poskovic and Const. Vincent Washington are each charged with manslaughter and assault causing bodily harm [1][2]. The officers were arrested Monday morning and released on an undertaking [1][2]. They are expected to appear in the Alberta Court of Justice in Calgary on Jan. 6, 2027 [1]. The Alberta Crown Prosecution Service advised that the charges be laid, according to the Canadian Press report [2].

The case goes back to Sept. 17, 2024, when police were called just before 1 a.m. to the Carriage House Hotel and Conference Centre at 9030 Macleod Trail S.E. for a man who was causing a disturbance and refusing to leave the lobby [1]. The police service's own release at the time said officers tried to de-escalate, then used a conductive energy weapon and later pepper spray when he did not co-operate, and that he went into medical distress after being taken into custody and was declared dead at the scene [1].

ASIRT's account, as reported by the Canadian Press, adds that the man appeared dazed, raised his hands and began to walk out, was taken to the ground after resisting an officer who tried to grab him, was punched in the head, restrained and sedated, and was later found unresponsive by emergency crews [2]. The watchdog said its investigation found reasonable grounds to believe offences were committed, and that the man was never told he was being detained or under arrest [2]. None of these allegations has been tested in court.

In an emailed statement, the Calgary Police Service said the charges raise questions of police accountability, the use of force and public trust, and called them "extremely serious" [1]. Both the police service and ASIRT said they could not comment further because the matter is now before the courts [1].

At the time of the death, Blood Tribe Chief Roy Fox said in a video statement that the community again found itself in a similar situation, and pointed to a public inquiry in the 1980s that examined the gap between the community and police [2].

articles.title: Budget hearing opens as a councillor asks to see what a zero per cent tax increase would look like
articles.dek: Council began hearing public submissions and debating on the proposed 2027-2030 budget, which calls for a 15 per cent rise in municipal property tax revenue in 2027.
body: Calgary city council resumed debate on its four-year budget on Monday, Nov. 23, as administration presented the proposed 2027-2030 plan again and the public hearing began [1][2]. Monday was the first day Calgarians could address council on the plan, which could bring significant property tax increases [2].

The proposal released on Nov. 10 includes $6 billion in operating spending for 2027 and $21 billion in recommended capital over four years, $13 billion of it new [3]. It calls for a 15 per cent increase in municipal property tax revenue from existing properties in 2027 [3]. For a typical single residential property, the City estimates that works out to about $37 a month more in municipal property tax and about $16 a month more for water, waste and recycling, or roughly $53 a month combined [3].

Ward 1 Coun. Kim Tyers said on Monday she wants administration to come back with a scenario showing a zero per cent property tax increase [1]. Over the summer, council had asked for previews of four-year increases of 15, 12.5, 9 and 6 per cent, and gave no direction on other scenarios [1].

Councillors were divided on the idea. Ward 14 Coun. Landon Johnston said council should have been voting on a five per cent option, while Ward 7 Coun. Myke Atkinson called choosing zero per cent irresponsible and said councillors have had the budget documents since July [1]. Atkinson also said property tax collection has fallen behind inflation and population growth over six years [1].

Mayor Jeromy Farkas said a zero per cent increase is always possible but comes with a cost, and that an increase of four to five per cent is needed to keep services running and keep up with infrastructure work [1]. Asked why council was not given other scenarios, he said, "Well, that's council's job, right?" [1]. When the plan was released, Farkas described it as a starting point rather than the final word [3].

The largest items in the proposal include $1.7 billion for the Pine Creek and Fish Creek wastewater plants, $616 million more for water infrastructure, $420 million for pavement rehabilitation, $300 million for RouteAhead buses and $192 million for police facilities and equipment [3]. Deliberations continue through the week, with final approval to follow debate [1][3].

articles.title: Road repair, transit and snow clearing among the spending questions as budget talks begin
articles.dek: The proposed budget sets aside $420 million for pavement over four years, but some councillors want more for roads and have floated shifting money from transit.
body: As council began its budget deliberations this week, road condition and transit funding are among the items drawing debate [1][2]. The City's proposed 2027-2030 budget includes about $420 million for pavement rehabilitation, $300 million for RouteAhead buses, $94 million for the Mobility Safety and Speed Management Program, $142 million for an interchange at 194 Avenue and Macleod Trail, and $71 million to extend the Blue Line to 88 Avenue N.E. [2].

Over four years, the City proposes $420.2 million for road rehabilitation, $178.1 million for bridge upgrades, $44 million for major road construction and $29.5 million for concrete rehabilitation, Global News reported [1]. City figures cited in that report show 11 per cent of city infrastructure in poor condition, and 38 per cent of roadways in good or better condition at the end of 2025, compared with a national average of 61 per cent [1].

Troy McLeod, the City's director of mobility, said rebuilding a road costs seven to 10 times more than resurfacing it, and that the network covers more than 17,000 lane-kilometres [1]. Crews had filled 35,641 potholes so far this year, he said [1]. Snow and ice control would rise by $7 million under the plan; McLeod said Calgary's budget for that work is just over $58 million, compared with $73 million in Edmonton [1].

Ward 10 Coun. Andre Chabot said the proposal does not deliver on pavement quality and that he is looking at moving money from Calgary Transit's budget requests to road maintenance, arguing that ridership is down and cost recovery is low [1]. Calgary Transit is asking for an extra $62 million in operating money for RouteAhead and $300 million in capital over four years for buses and renewal [1].

Alex Williams of the group Calgary Transit Riders said cutting transit would push more people into cars and add wear to roads [1]. Matti Siemiatycki, director of the University of Toronto's Infrastructure Institute, told Global News that putting money into maintenance is critical [1]. No decisions have been made; deliberations continue this week [1][2].

articles.title: Water restrictions expected to lift in about a week and a half as Bearspaw work enters third week
articles.dek: Weekend demand stayed under the 500-million-litre limit, and the City says WinSport can make some snow overnight while the new feeder main is connected.
body: Work to connect the new Bearspaw South Feeder Main entered its third week on schedule, and the City of Calgary said on Monday, Nov. 23 that water restrictions are expected to be lifted in about a week and a half [1]. Stage 4 restrictions remained in place over the weekend [2].

Water use in Calgary and the region stayed well below the 500-million-litre daily target, at 476 million litres on Saturday and 490 million litres on Sunday, the City said [1]. The target covers Calgary, Airdrie, Chestermere, Strathmore and Tsuut'ina Nation [1].

At the Shaganappi Pump Station, the pipe connection is finished and a valve chamber is being installed [1]. At 89 Street and 33 Avenue, crews working around the clock have placed a new steel T-joint and connected it to the existing pipe that leads to the Bearspaw Water Treatment Plant, with welding still under way [1]. At 83 Street and 33 Avenue the excavation was widened to expose existing distribution pipes, but the City said the work remains on schedule [1]. Pipe installation is complete at all five locations at Parkdale Boulevard and Memorial Drive N.W., where backfilling and surface repair are under way [1].

The City also said WinSport, a not-for-profit, may make snow overnight using up to 3 million litres of water a night when the weather allows [1]. That permission can be withdrawn at any time if demand climbs too high or problems arise in the system [1]. Even after restrictions lift, WinSport will be limited to about 40 per cent of its full snowmaking capacity until the new feeder main is fully in service, which the City expects in mid to late December [1].

articles.title: Advocates warn proposed budget would stall new tree planting after 2028
articles.dek: Federal tree-planting money runs out in 2028 and the proposed 2027-2030 budget lists no replacement, leaving only funds to replace dead trees.
body: Climate advocates say growth in Calgary's tree canopy would stall if the proposed 2027-2030 budget passes as written, LiveWire Calgary reported on Nov. 22 [1]. The canopy covers just under 10 per cent of the city, against a target of 16 per cent by 2060 [1].

Calgary's tree-planting work has been backed by the federal 2 Billion Trees program, which has contributed $61 million in total [1]. To keep that money, the City must fund $12 million in planting in each of 2027 and 2028, or it would lose $11.3 million in federal funding [1]. The program aims to plant 930,000 trees by 2039; nearly 360,000 have been planted so far, and about 500,000 more are expected by 2028 [1].

According to the budget documents, that funding ends by 2028 and no replacement is listed, with the document noting that further investment is required [1]. The $54.4-million urban forestry lifecycle budget covers only replacing and removing dead trees, meaning no net-new trees would be planted after 2029, and the Branching Out program is unfunded in 2029 and 2030 [1].

Rob Miller, a volunteer with the Calgary Climate Hub, said his group had planned to ask for $10 million for tree equity work and that the amount needed has nearly doubled [1]. He described his reaction to the budget with the words "My jaw dropped" [1].
Public submissions on the budget opened on Monday, Nov. 23, the same day council resumed its four-year budget debate [1][2]. Council has not yet voted on any part of the plan [2].

articles.title: Alberta tables natural gas pipeline bill as Calgary-based TC Energy warns of risk to expansion
articles.dek: The Natural Gas Infrastructure Act would let the province set up a Crown entity to build gas transmission as a last resort if private industry does not.
body: The Alberta government introduced the Natural Gas Infrastructure Act on Monday, Nov. 23, legislation that would give the province a larger role in planning and supporting gas pipelines and more competition in a network dominated by Calgary-based TC Energy [1][2]. The bill does not itself create any Crown corporation, but it sets a framework for one to take part in gas transmission if private industry fails to build, which the government describes as a last resort [1][2].

Energy and Minerals Minister Brian Jean told reporters that pipeline capacity is becoming a constraint on growth as demand rises from data centres and the oilsands [2]. He said TC Energy's NGTL network, the backbone of the system, is fully subscribed until 2029, and that he was encouraged by the company's expansion plans announced Nov. 16, which include a new 370-kilometre pipeline to the oilsands region [2]. The government's earlier modelling put possible demand above planned capacity by 1.3 to 5.1 billion cubic feet a day by 2034 [1].

In a letter to Premier Danielle Smith dated Nov. 21, TC Energy president and chief executive François Poirier warned the bill could undermine planned investment, create significant market instability and lead to duplication [1][2]. He wrote that the company would struggle to advance its newly announced expansion of more than 1.3 billion cubic feet a day if the law overrides the existing system [1]. TC Energy met provincial officials on Nov. 19 and was told the changes would proceed [2]. The Hub reported, citing unnamed sources, that the company is exploring legal options; that has not been confirmed by the company [1].

The bill does not spell out what would trigger government intervention or how a Crown entity would be financed, according to The Hub [1]. A cabinet document first reported by The Narwhal had described TC Energy's dominance as a market failure and flagged possible court challenges as legal considerations [2]. The NGTL system has been under federal jurisdiction since 2009, which could complicate the province's plans [1].
Jean said TC Energy should not treat the bill as an ultimatum [2]. The Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers said it looks forward to reviewing the legislation [1].

articles.dek: The club brought back receiver Matt Sibley and offensive linemen Mitchel Schechinger and Jack Warrack from its 2026 Canadian Draft class.
body: The Calgary Stampeders announced on Monday, Nov. 23 that they have re-signed three players from their 2026 CFL Canadian Draft class: receiver Matt Sibley and offensive linemen Mitchel Schechinger and Jack Warrack [1]. The club did not release contract terms [1].

Sibley, a Calgary native and graduate of Ernest Manning High School, was taken in the fifth round, 44th overall [1]. He was placed on the retired list on July 7 so he could return to the University of Calgary, where he caught 51 passes for 938 yards and six touchdowns last season and was named a Canada West all-star [1]. Over five seasons with the Dinos from 2022 to 2026, he had 156 receptions, 2,240 yards and 13 touchdowns, a program record, according to the team [1].

Schechinger, from Sarnia, Ont., was a sixth-round pick, 53rd overall, out of the University of Guelph, where he played 27 games from 2022 to 2026 and was a first-team Ontario University Athletics all-star in 2024 and 2026 [1].

Warrack, from Strathmore, was chosen in the eighth round, 71st overall, from the University of Saskatchewan [1]. He was the Canada West rookie of the year in 2022 and a conference all-star in 2024 [1].

articles.title: Cavalry FC beats Atletico Ottawa 3-2 at Spruce Meadows to win the CPL's first league-and-championship double
articles.dek: Tobias Warschewski scored twice as Calgary's club won the North Star Cup before a record 9,131 fans, adding the title to its regular-season Shield.
body: Cavalry FC won the Canadian Premier League championship on Saturday, Nov. 21, beating Atletico Ottawa 3-2 in the CPL Final at ATCO Field at Spruce Meadows [1][2]. The win made Cavalry the first club in the league's eight-year history to take both the regular-season CPL Shield and the North Star Cup, the championship trophy, in the same season [1][2][3].

Tobias Warschewski opened the scoring in the fifth minute [1][2]. Sergio Camargo made it 2-0 in the 47th minute, heading in a cross from Warschewski [1]. Ottawa cut the lead in the 65th minute when the ball went in off a Cavalry defender for an own goal [1][2]. Warschewski restored the two-goal margin in the 74th minute, and Nicolas Fleuriau Chateau scored from the penalty spot for Ottawa deep in stoppage time, too late to change the result [1][2][3].

Warschewski, the league's player of the year, was named the match's most valuable player after two goals and an assist [1][2]. The Canadian Press reported that his second goal was his eighth in eight career playoff games, the most in the league [1].

The crowd of 9,131 was a club record for ATCO Field, according to the league's release, which said more than 16,000 people were on the Spruce Meadows grounds that day [2]. The Canadian Press described a wind chill of minus 11 C, with some fans sitting on a snowbank beside the field [1].

The game was a rematch of the 2025 final, which Ottawa won 2-1 in extra time during a snowstorm at TD Place in Ottawa [1][3]. Cavalry reached the final for a fourth straight year and won its second North Star Cup, after its first in 2024 [1][3]. The league said Cavalry finished first in the 2026 regular season with 60 points from 18 wins, six draws and four losses, scored a league-record 58 goals and went unbeaten at home [2].

Ottawa played without its leading scorer, who was injured in the semifinal against Hamilton, according to The Canadian Press [1]. Cavalry is coached by Tommy Wheeldon Jr. and has played in the league since its first season in 2019 [2]. CTV News also reported the 3-2 result [4].

articles.title: Premier Smith says amendments are coming to Alberta's bike lane bill after pushback from Calgary and Edmonton
articles.dek: Danielle Smith said Saturday the province has changes to propose to Bill 43, a day after her transportation minister said cities would pay for ordered bike lane removals.
body: Premier Danielle Smith said on Saturday, Nov. 21, that her government has amendments to propose to Bill 43, the Safe and Sensible Roads Act, the transportation bill that would give the province power over municipal bike lanes [1]. Speaking on her Saturday morning radio show, Smith said her chief of staff met Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas during the week about concerns she called legitimate, and that she wants a collaborative process with cities [1].

The bill was introduced on Thursday, Nov. 19, by Transportation Minister Devin Dreeshen [1][2]. As introduced, it would bar municipalities from installing new bike lanes that remove or restrict road space for vehicles without the minister's written approval, and would let the minister order existing bike lanes removed [1][2]. It would also expand provincial powers over municipal LRT projects, including the ability to approve plans and direct changes at any stage, even during construction [1].

The new development is the premier's statement. On Friday, Farkas said the bill appeared to have been fumbled and that it did not reflect assurances from the premier's office that the province would cover the cost of any removals it ordered [2]. He described the published text as a premature draft and said he expected changes, including to the minister-approval requirement [2]. The same day, Dreeshen told reporters that municipalities would be responsible for paying for removals the province orders, according to the Calgary Herald [1]. Smith did not say on Saturday what the amendments would contain [1].

Smith said the province would work with municipalities to identify bike lanes that are underused or interfere with traffic, and to decide whether to modify or remove them when road construction begins [1]. On LRT, she pointed to cost overruns and said the province needs a role as a funding partner; she also raised fare collection and passenger safety [1].

In an emailed statement reported by CBC, Dreeshen said the province would work with cities to limit future bike lanes in busy areas and deal with lanes it considers problems, and suggested removals be timed to scheduled road work to save money [2]. The ministry did not directly address the mayor's account or confirm amendments in that statement [2].

Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack also criticized the bill, saying the province should focus on its own responsibilities [1][2]. Edmonton city administration has estimated that removing that city's bike lanes could cost $150 million [1][2]. Cycling groups in both cities, including Bike Calgary, have opposed the bill [2].

articles.title: Police and sheriffs issue 149 summonses in three-night downtown Calgary operation
articles.dek: A joint Calgary Police Service and Alberta Sheriffs operation from Nov. 13 to 15 also led to 10 charges, six warrants and two drug trafficking investigations.
body: Calgary Police Service officers and Alberta Sheriffs issued 149 summonses and laid 10 charges during a three-night enforcement operation in downtown Calgary, police said in results released Thursday, Nov. 19 [1][2]. The operation ran on evening shifts from Friday, Nov. 13, to Sunday, Nov. 15 [1][2].

Police said officers executed six arrest warrants and conducted about 400 mandatory alcohol screenings at checkstops [1][2]. Nine drivers received immediate roadside sanctions: four for failing impaired driving tests and five for impaired driving warnings [1][2]. Officers also carried out two commercial vehicle inspections [1].

Two drug trafficking investigations were opened, and police said officers seized crack cocaine, fentanyl, methamphetamine, Xanax and OxyContin [1][2]. Neither the police release nor news reports gave the amounts seized, and police did not break down the 10 charges by offence [1][2].

Police said officers and sheriffs focused on hot spots known for social disorder and drug use, but did not name specific locations [1][2]. Acting Insp. Paul Ralstin of the police service's District 1 and Alberta Sheriffs Insp. Bj Bjornson both commented on the joint work, with Bjornson saying, "Albertans expect law enforcement agencies to work together" [1].

Police said the operation is part of Safer Calgary, an ongoing initiative that combines enforcement and patrols with social supports [1][2]. The Medicine Hat News reported that a one-day sweep earlier in November led to 10 people being charged and 99 summonses, and that police reported in August that downtown violence was at a six-year high [2].

articles.title: Owner and contractor of downtown Hanover Building fined more than $120,000 after equipment fell to the street
articles.dek: Two companies pleaded guilty to building and fire code violations after a 70-pound metal shroud blew off the building during repairs in 2025; no one was hurt.
body: Two companies connected to a construction project at the Hanover Building in downtown Calgary have been fined more than $120,000 for building and fire code violations, the City of Calgary said in a release posted Nov. 19 [1].
The City said that on April 29, 2025, a 70-pound metal shroud covering ventilation equipment blew off the building while it was under repair and fell to the street below [1]. No one was injured [1].

On Sept. 23, 2026, the Alberta Court of Justice accepted guilty pleas from the property owner, 101 Residential Capital, and the general contractor, Cairo Development Ltd., according to the City [1]. The City said the pleas relate to violations of the National Building Code and the National Fire Code, and that the companies admitted proper precautions were not taken to prevent undue risk to the public and that several fire code requirements were not met [1]. The release did not say how the fines were split between the two companies [1].

The City said its own investigations led to the prosecutions [1]. Darren Lockhart, the City's manager of building and development inspections, said, "The safety of residents, visitors and workers must always come first" [1]. Virginia Buckley, deputy chief of risk management with the Calgary Fire Department, also commented in the release [1].

The City said its safety codes officers enforce building and fire rules on construction sites, and that it is working on construction-site safety planning, guidance for the industry and stronger enforcement tools [1]. The release did not give the building's street address [1].

articles.title: Calgary man pleads guilty to threatening to kill the prime minister and his family
articles.dek: A 31-year-old Calgary man admitted to posting online threats against Prime Minister Mark Carney, along with charges tied to an attack on a tire shop.
body: A 31-year-old Calgary man pleaded guilty in a Calgary courtroom on Friday, November 20, to threatening to kill Prime Minister Mark Carney and members of his family, The Canadian Press reported [1].

Jamie Dacosta pleaded guilty to four criminal charges [1]. Along with the threat against the prime minister, he admitted to uttering threats, extortion and mischief involving a Calgary tire shop and its staff, where video shows him smashing windows with an axe, according to the report [1].

The threats against Carney were made in online posts, including videos on YouTube and TikTok [1]. Calgary police and the RCMP's Integrated National Security Enforcement Team learned of a threat posted on YouTube, and Dacosta was arrested in September [1]. The report says Calgary police had warned him in March after a TikTok video in which he said he would harm the prime minister and kill one of his children [1]. His last post came a few days before Carney was scheduled to visit Red Deer, north of Calgary [1].
The videos were played in court, and the report says Dacosta yawned and laughed while they were shown [1].

Defence lawyer Adriano Iovinelli asked the court to order a pre-sentence report [1]. He described the comments as alarming, said his client had made clear the posts were his own, and suggested his client should be assessed for mental illness [1]. No Crown position on sentence was reported [1].

No sentencing date has been set. The case returns to court on February 4, and the Crown has time to find out whether the prime minister wishes to provide a victim impact statement, according to the report [1].

articles.title: Calgary Transit moving its whole bus fleet to all-weather tires after a pilot cut stuck buses by 45 per cent
articles.dek: About half of Calgary's 40- and 60-foot buses already run on all-weather tires, and the rest are due to switch by the end of 2027.
body: Calgary Transit says fewer of its buses should get stuck on snowy roads this winter, after a pilot found all-weather tires sharply reduced traction problems [1].

Last winter, the agency compared 11 buses fitted with all-season tires against 11 fitted with all-weather tires, running on routes with known winter trouble spots [1]. Buses on all-weather tires had 45 per cent fewer stuck-bus incidents [1].
Calgary Transit said that during one four-day stretch with more than 10 centimetres of snow, 100 buses got stuck across the fleet, and the units with all-weather tires got stuck less often [1].

About half of the 40- and 60-foot bus fleet, roughly 500 buses, now runs on all-weather tires, and the whole fleet is expected to have them by the end of 2027 [1]. The agency began replacing worn or damaged all-season tires with all-weather tires last year [1]. It says the approach avoids extra spending on second sets of tires, seasonal changeovers, storage and inventory, since the buses do not need to swap tires each season [1].

Calgary Transit also listed other winter measures. Routes with traction trouble spots get priority for snow clearing under The City's Priority Snow Plan, and the longer 60-foot articulated buses are limited in snowy conditions [1].

articles.title: Alberta opens $250-million round to build more than 2,000 affordable homes
articles.dek: Housing providers across the province, including in Calgary, can apply until January 31, 2027, for help covering up to one-third of project costs.
body: The Alberta government announced on Friday, November 20, that it is committing $250 million to a new round of its Affordable Housing Partnership Program, with the aim of building more than 2,000 new affordable homes [1].

The round is open now and applications close January 31, 2027 [1]. Public, non-profit and private-sector housing providers can apply for projects that build, buy, convert or expand housing [1]. Provincial support can cover up to one-third of eligible project costs, and at least 10 per cent of units in each project must be accessible [1].

The program launched in 2022 under Stronger Foundations, the province's 10-year affordable housing plan [1]. The province says about $730 million has been committed through the program so far, for more than 7,400 new affordable homes and more than 630 shelter spaces [1].

The government says it is more than 70 per cent of the way to the plan's goal of serving 25,000 additional households by 2031, which it describes as ahead of schedule [1]. It also says about 64,500 affordable housing units are supported across Alberta, helping about 122,000 people, and that it has put $2 billion in capital funding into affordable housing, seniors housing and continuing care spaces since 2019 [1].

The release was issued by Assisted Living and Social Services Minister Nathan Neudorf's ministry [1]. It does not say how much of the new round is expected to go to Calgary projects; funding is awarded through applications from providers [1].

The agreement is tied to the government's goal of growing annual visitor spending in Alberta to $25 billion by 2035 [1]. articles.title: University of Calgary study calls for round-the-clock family access in children's intensive care
articles.dek: Researchers led by an Alberta Children's Hospital nurse-scientist say limits on family visits in pediatric ICUs can harm patients and families.
body: New research from a University of Calgary program recommends that children in pediatric intensive care units have access to two designated support people at all hours, LiveWire Calgary reported on November 20 [1].

The study, published earlier this month in JAMA Network Open, drew on surveys and interviews with 43 people from across Canada, including former patients, family members, clinicians and policymakers [1]. Pediatric ICUs treat patients from infancy to age 18 [1].

The work was led by Laurie Lee, an associate professor of nursing at the University of Calgary and director of the Alberta Children's Hospital PICU Research Program, with co-author Jennifer Foster of Dalhousie University [1]. The two began the research during the COVID-19 pandemic, when restrictions on family presence in intensive care units took effect [1]. It follows an earlier University of Calgary study on family togetherness for adult patients [1].

According to the report, participants said family presence helped patients, families and health-care workers, including with coping, healing and shorter stays [1]. Lee told LiveWire that having families at the bedside actually decreases workload for staff [1]. Families described limits on visiting hours and on the number of visitors, which Lee said were harmful to both patients and families [1].
The research did not support the idea that limiting contact between members of the same household reduced the spread of infectious disease, according to the report [1].

The authors recommend that patients and families help write visiting policies [1]. Hospital boards usually set these guidelines, though provincial or federal governments can override them during a health emergency [1]. The researchers plan to present their findings to policymakers at the Children's Healthcare Canada conference in April 2027 [1].

articles.title: Farkas invites premier and prime minister to Calgary to talk about costs passed down to the city
articles.dek: Days before budget debate begins, the mayor says provincial and federal costs make up nearly a third of the proposed 15 per cent property tax increase.
body: Mayor Jeromy Farkas has formally invited Premier Danielle Smith and Prime Minister Mark Carney to a three-way meeting in Calgary on costs he says other orders of government have shifted onto the city [1].

The invitation comes as council prepares to start deliberations on the next four-year city budget on Monday, Nov. 23 [1]. The proposed budget calls for a 15 per cent property tax increase in 2027, which works out to about $53 a month for a typical single-family detached homeowner, and water rates that would rise by nearly 75 per cent by 2030 [1].

Farkas pointed to a figure in the city's own budget documents that puts provincially and federally downloaded costs at $137.5 million in 2027 [1]. He said that amount equals about 5.6 percentage points of the proposed tax increase, or nearly a third of the total [1]. The article's summary line gives the figure as roughly $135 million, while the body uses $137.5 million [1].

The mayor also said federal counter-tariffs in the trade dispute with the United States could add between $355 million and $466 million to city costs, which he described as equivalent to an 18 per cent property tax increase [1]. He said he wants all three orders of government at the same table [1].

Not every councillor sees value in the meeting. Ward 11 Coun. Rob Ward said costs are downloaded only because the city allows it, citing the low-income transit pass that the city pays for [1]. He questioned whether a meeting would help, noting that Farkas and Ward 13 Coun. Dan McLean travelled to Ottawa in February and that promised help for infrastructure and transit has not yet arrived [1].
The Government of Alberta was sent the list of downloaded costs from the budget but had not responded when the report was published [1]. No response from the federal government was reported [1].

articles.title: Council votes 11-4 to map unused city space that non-profits could rent below market
articles.dek: A motion from Ward 8 Coun. Nathan Schmidt starts work on a framework for offering city-owned space to community groups.
body: Calgary city council voted 11-4 on Tuesday, Nov. 17 to have city administration begin work on a framework that would make city-owned space available to local non-profits at below-market rates [1].

The motion, brought by Ward 8 Coun. Nathan Schmidt, calls for an inventory of city-owned space that community organizations could use and a process for handling requests for it [1]. The idea grew out of the case of the Arusha Centre, which was given notice to leave the Old Y building in the Beltline; the group later submitted a plan to revitalize that site [1].

Schmidt argued the city can help community groups without spending money, and said non-profits taking over vacant space could save the city maintenance costs such as plumbing and heating and ventilation [1].

Calgary's Non-Profit Chamber sent a letter of support. Alexa Briggs, the chamber's executive vice president of policy, insight and engagement, said rising overhead costs were the second-highest concern in its 2025 research on the sector [1].

Opponents raised cost concerns. Ward 13 Coun. Dan McLean said the number of non-profits is growing quickly and subsidizing them has a cost [1]. Ward 12 Coun. Mike Jamieson said he would not support what he described as the start of a new subsidy program during budget month [1]. Ward 9 Coun. Harrison Clark backed the motion as a way to help non-profits at no cost to the city [1].
Administration is to bring a series of reports through 2027, with a final report due in the first quarter of 2028 [1].

articles.title: Farkas says Calgary will not pay to remove bike lanes under Bill 43; ministry has not confirmed
articles.dek: The mayor says the premier's office assured him the city is not on the hook, a day after the province tabled its omnibus roads bill.
body: A day after the province tabled a transportation bill that could lead to some bike lanes being removed, Mayor Jeromy Farkas said he has been assured that Calgary will not have to pay for any removals [1]. Alberta's transportation ministry did not confirm that on Friday, Nov. 20 [1].
Bill 43, the Safe and Sensible Roads Act, was tabled on Thursday, Nov. 19. It covers bike lanes, personal mobility devices, changes to LRT design and other matters [1].

Farkas told reporters the premier's office told him the bike-lane section of the bill as first drafted was a premature version and a mistake, and that an updated version focuses on future bike lanes rather than existing ones [1]. He said municipalities would not pay for removals under any circumstances [1].

As first proposed, the bill would require a case, supported by data, that a new bike lane would not reduce road capacity. It also said the province was reviewing bike lanes in Calgary and Edmonton and that some could be removed, especially when roads are repaved or resurfaced [1].

Transportation Minister Devin Dreeshen said on Thursday the province would not pay for removals, which Farkas said was not the message he had received [1]. In an emailed statement on Friday, the ministry said it would limit future bike lanes in high-traffic areas and deal with existing problem lanes in co-operation with the municipalities affected; the statement did not say who would pay [1].

Dreeshen named a southwest Calgary route, which LiveWire Calgary linked to the 26 Avenue S.W. bike lane, a project that removed a substantial number of parking spaces [1]. Who pays for any removals remains unresolved, as the mayor's account and the ministry's statements do not match [1].

articles.title: Water use under the limit for a 16th straight day as Bearspaw crews connect a new steel joint
articles.dek: Calgary used 480 million litres on Thursday, and the City says snow and cold are not expected to slow the feeder main work.
body: Calgary and neighbouring communities kept water use in the green zone for a 16th straight day, the City said Friday, Nov. 20, as Stage 4 water restrictions continue [1][2].

Water use on Thursday, Nov. 19 was 480 million litres, two million litres below forecast demand [1]. The City is asking residents to keep daily demand below 500 million litres, which keeps the system out of the red zone, where less water would be available for emergencies and everyday services [1].

Connection work on the new Bearspaw feeder main is moving ahead at three sites [1]. At 33 Avenue and 89 Street N.W., where crews are working around the clock, a new steel joint has been placed and connected, linking the new feeder main to the existing pipe that leads to the Bearspaw Water Treatment Plant; welding continues [1]. At 33 Avenue and 83 Street N.W., the excavation has been widened to allow extra work on an existing pipe, and pipe installation and welding continue near the Shaganappi Pump Station [1].

Separate repairs along Parkdale Boulevard, between the Shaganappi and Memorial pump stations, are also progressing. The City said pipe installation was to be finished at all those locations on Friday, with backfilling through the weekend [1].

The update comes as Calgary heads into what CTV News describes as its first winter weekend, with a cold Friday morning and traces of snow expected [3]. The City said snow and colder weather are not expected to delay the project and that crews will keep working through winter conditions [1].

articles.title: Fireworks calls fall 65 per cent over Diwali as City credits outreach with faith and cultural groups
articles.dek: Police and 311 logged 72 fireworks-related calls over the three-day period, down from more than 207 last year.
body: Fireworks-related calls during this year's Diwali and Bandi Chhor Divas celebrations dropped by 65 per cent compared with 2025, the City of Calgary said Thursday, Nov. 19 [1].
Calgary police and 311 received 72 fireworks-related calls and service requests over the three-day Diwali period, down from more than 207 during the same period last year [1].

There were five fireworks-related fires this year, all involving grass or dumpsters, compared with six in 2025, which included a vehicle fire and a fire on a residential balcony [1]. The City said this year's fires caused less damage, with no harm to buildings or neighbouring properties, even though conditions were unusually dry and windy [1].

Police and Community Safety peace officers issued eight tickets and 70 warnings [1]. Business safety staff visited 115 businesses and found none selling fireworks illegally, which the City called an improvement over previous years [1].

The City said it worked with faith groups, cultural organizations and community members on an education campaign in several languages, and a community-organized professional fireworks display was held at the Diwali in Huxley event on Nov. 5 [1]. Fire Marshal Glenn Baxter called the results encouraging [1].

Personal fireworks are not permitted in Calgary; only trained, certified professionals with a permit may set them off [1]. The City asks people to call 9-1-1 for fires or emergencies, the police non-emergency line at 403-266-1234 for fireworks happening now, and to file a 311 request for fireworks that have already happened [1].

body: The City of Calgary presented the 2026 Mayor's Urban Design Awards on Wednesday, Nov. 18 at The Ampersand, recognizing buildings, public spaces, plans and student work across the city [1].

articles.title: Alberta lets carbon capture grants flow during construction, matching the federal tax credit
articles.dek: The change to the province's incentive program comes as talks on the Pathways project run past a mid-November target.
body: Alberta has changed its carbon capture and storage incentive so that some money can be paid while projects are being built, not only once they start operating [1][2].

Under the Alberta Carbon Capture Incentive Program, companies can receive grants covering 12 per cent of eligible capital costs for certain projects, including in the oil and gas, petrochemical and power industries [1][2]. The province said the change brings its program in line with the federal Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage Tax Credit [1][2].
Energy and Minerals Minister Brian Jean announced the change in a news release late Thursday, Nov. 19, describing Alberta as already a global leader in carbon capture and storage [1].

The change comes as Alberta, Ottawa and the five biggest oilsands producers negotiate final agreements on the Pathways project [1][2]. The governments and industry had aimed to announce those agreements around Nov. 15, but company executives have signalled they will take the time they need [1][2].

Pathways would carry carbon dioxide by pipeline from oilsands sites to an underground storage hub near Cold Lake [1][2]. The Oil Sands Alliance, made up of Cenovus Energy, Canadian Natural Resources, Suncor Energy, Imperial Oil and ConocoPhillips Canada, is developing the project [1].

The project would be able to store about six million tonnes of captured carbon dioxide a year by the mid-2030s, with another 10 million tonnes of reductions targeted by 2045, a significant scale-back from the 22 million tonnes by 2030 targeted earlier [1]. Under a federal-provincial energy accord signed a year ago, progress on Pathways is tied to Ottawa's support for the proposed Pacific Link pipeline to the West Coast, and the reverse [1].

articles.title: Alberta tables bill giving the province power over city bike lanes
articles.dek: Bill 43 would bar new bike lanes that take road space from vehicles without the transportation minister's approval and let the province order existing lanes removed.
body: The Alberta government tabled legislation on Thursday, Nov. 19, that would give the province control over municipal bike lanes in Calgary, Edmonton and other cities [1][2]. Transportation and Economic Corridors Minister Devin Dreeshen introduced Bill 43, the Safe and Sensible Roads Act 2026 [1][2].

If the bill passes, municipalities could not install a new bike lane that removes or restricts road capacity for vehicles unless the minister gives written approval [1][2]. The minister could also order the removal of existing bike lanes that reduce capacity for motor vehicles, and could return them to vehicle use during road work [2]. Municipalities could ask for exemptions, which would be judged case by case, with the minister making the final decision [2]. The bill sets no criteria for the minister's decisions [1].

Dreeshen said the province will ask Calgary and Edmonton for data on certain bike lanes, including traffic impact assessments of those roads and nearby roads, and then decide with the municipalities whether a lane makes sense [2]. A provincial bike lane portal this summer drew 14,000 responses, and 26 Street in Calgary was among the 10 most-reported lanes; the other nine on the list are in Edmonton [2]. Officials said the bill does not set out an exact removal process [2]. The Canadian Press reported the bill does not say who would pay for removals, while the Edmonton Journal reported that cities would bear the cost [1][2]. Asked about funding, Dreeshen said, "We do not have a provincial bike lane budget" [2].

The bill also covers other transportation matters. It would raise penalties for unsafe commercial trucking operators and create provincial safety standards for privately owned e-scooters, one-wheels and similar personal devices [1][2]. The province is considering helmet rules and possible limits on speed, power and weight, with the standards due in early 2027 and taking effect April 1, 2027; municipalities would keep bylaw authority over how the devices operate [2]. The bill would also align municipal LRT projects with the province's Passenger Rail Master Plan [2].

Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas spoke against provincial intervention in bike lanes, and Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack raised concerns about costs passed to taxpayers [1]. Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi told the province to stay out of the issue [2]. Cycling advocates warned that removing lanes would put cyclists at risk [1]. Details are to be set in regulations, which the Canadian Press reported are expected to take effect in the spring [1].
