articles.title: Province's data centre bill sets 600-metre buffer from homes; Calgary councillors call it a good start
articles.dek: Bill 42 would keep large data centres away from homes and top farmland and make the Alberta Utilities Commission their main regulator, a day after Calgary council moved on its own rules.
body: The Alberta government has tabled Bill 42, the Energy, Environment and Utilities Statutes Amendment Act, 2026, which would set province-wide rules for where large data centres can be built [1][2]. Technology and Innovation Minister Nate Glubish tabled the omnibus bill in the legislature on Wednesday, Nov. 18 [1][4].

Under the bill, data centres of 10 megawatts or more could not be built within 600 metres of a home, on irrigated land or on high-quality farmland [1][2][4]. The province says that protects about 14 million acres of farmland [2][4]. Municipalities may set larger setbacks, and the 600-metre distance is a minimum [1][3]. Sites in designated industrial zones, on brownfield land or at existing power plants would not need the setback [1][4]. Projects under 10 megawatts would stay with municipalities [4].

The Alberta Utilities Commission would be the main regulator for data centres of 10 megawatts and up, and would apply the same noise and light standards used for power plants [2][4]. The bill would let the province set water-efficiency standards aimed at bringing cooling water use to near zero, with details to come in regulations [3][4]. Data centre proponents would have to pay for the grid infrastructure they need [2][3]. Officials say 70 proposals are in the province's program and up to 30 per cent could be affected [2][4]. Projects already approved or well underway, including Meta's planned $13-billion campus near Edmonton, would be exempt [1][4]. The bill also covers oil and gas cleanup, illegal dumping penalties and forestry, and repeals the Oil Sands Emissions Limit Act [2].

In Calgary, councillors said the rules could address local concerns about water, power and noise [3]. Council voted on Tuesday to study the effects of large data centres and pursue land-use bylaw changes [3]. Ward 5 Coun. Raj Dhaliwal called the provincial rules a positive step but said they do not replace the city's own due diligence, and he wants a tool to pause emerging industries [3]. Ward 2 Coun. Jennifer Wyness called the rules a great start and welcomed that land-use decisions and public hearings stay with cities, while noting uncertainty about effects on residents and property values [3].

Critics want more. An Olds-area opponent has called for buffers of two to five kilometres [1], and NDP critic Nathan Ip said, "It's unclear if this government has actually consulted with municipalities" [4]. A July Leger poll cited by Global News found Canadians closely split on data centre development in their province [1].

articles.title: Calgary firefighters handle four fires in 24 hours, including an encampment tent fire
articles.dek: One person was taken to hospital with significant burns after a tent fire in the southeast, and another after a vehicle fire near Stoney Trail.
body: The Calgary Fire Department responded to four fires in about 24 hours on Tuesday, Nov. 17, and early Wednesday, Nov. 18, as heavy, wet snow fell on the city [1][2].

Shortly before 6 a.m. on Tuesday, crews were called to an occupied encampment in the 4400 block of Ogden Road S.E., where a tent was on fire [1][2]. Firefighters knocked the fire down quickly with a hose line [1]. One person, the tent's only occupant, had significant burn injuries and was taken to hospital by EHS after initial treatment [1]. A fire investigator found the fire started inside the tent [1].

Around 7:30 a.m., crews went to a single-vehicle fire off the road near Stoney Trail and Sun Valley Boulevard S.E. [1]. One person was found on the ground and was cared for by firefighters before being taken to hospital [1]. Crews found a damaged electrical vault near the collision and called Enmax to assess it, and the fire department left the scene with Calgary police [1]. A CJWE report placed the vehicle fire on Ashley Crescent, which differs from the fire department's account [2].

Just before 6 p.m., heavy smoke and fire were coming from a bedroom window of a single-storey home in the 300 block of Ashley Crescent S.E. [1][3]. Everyone inside got out on their own, one person was assessed on scene and not taken to hospital, and the fire was kept to the bedroom [1].

Around 4 a.m. Wednesday, a shed or playhouse-type structure at the rear of a property in the 100 block of Rundlehorn Crescent N.E. caught fire [1][2]. The occupants left on their own, the house was not damaged, and crews checked neighbouring garages for heat and damage [1]. No injuries were reported [1].
Investigators attended the house and shed fires [1]. The department used the release to remind families to practise a home escape plan twice a year [1].

articles.title: Man faces 15 charges after string of vehicle thefts and break-in attempts, police say
articles.dek: Calgary police say the man breached release conditions while committing thefts between mid-September and late October.
body: Calgary police have laid 15 charges against a 48-year-old man they describe as a prolific offender, following a series of thefts and attempted vehicle break-ins this fall [1][2].

Police say the man was released from custody in May and then breached his release conditions while committing offences between Monday, Sept. 14, and Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026 [1]. The alleged offences included attempted break-ins to vehicles, a theft from a recreation centre office and the use of stolen credit cards [1]. CTV News reported the case involved several car prowlings and thefts between mid-September and mid-October [2].
On Tuesday, Nov. 3, officers saw the man going into unlocked parked vehicles along 17 Avenue S.W. and arrested him, according to police [1].

Jonathan Keith Holmes, 48, is charged with two counts of theft under $5,000, one count of attempted theft under $5,000, two counts of using stolen credit cards, eight counts of breaching a release order, one count of attempted break and enter and one count of possession of a controlled substance [1]. None of the charges has been proven in court.
Police said he remained in custody and was scheduled to next appear in court on Thursday, Nov. 19 [1]. The outcome of that appearance was not available.

Police are asking anyone with information to call the non-emergency line at 403-266-1234 [1]. They also advised drivers to lock their vehicles and remove valuables, including wallets, purses and mail [1].

articles.title: Alberta Teachers' Association says recent education changes are causing 'chaos and confusion'
articles.dek: The teachers' union called for consultation before new legislation as school boards in Calgary wait for details on the new graduation rules.
body: The Alberta Teachers' Association criticized a series of recent provincial education decisions at a news conference on Thursday, Nov. 19, adding a formal union response to the debate over the province's new high school graduation rules [1].

ATA president Jason Schilling described the moves as political distractions [1]. He pointed to Bill 35, introduced in October, on reporting student achievement to families; the former Bill 25 from March on political neutrality in schools; and last week's updated graduation requirements [1]. He said the changes were introduced without consulting those who work in education, and asked for a clear, transparent process before new legislation is brought in [1]. He also urged the public to contact their MLAs [1].

Under the new rules, by 2030 Grade 11 and 12 students would need fewer core credits and have more room for electives [1]. Physical education would be required throughout high school, and a revised career and life management course would be needed to graduate [1]. The ATA raised concerns about literacy gaps and hurdles for students entering post-secondary, as well as staffing and gymnasium space [1].

Education and Childcare Minister Demetrios Nicolaides said on Nov. 13 that the graduation decision was partly informed by his student advisory council [1]. Asked in question period who he consulted, he cited several American research studies [1]. Premier Danielle Smith has defended the changes, while NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said they appeared to lower standards [1].

In Calgary, the Calgary Board of Education said it had not yet received details from the ministry, and the Calgary Catholic School District said it will assess the impacts [1]. No government timeline for further steps was given [1].

Calgary is 10-11-1 with 21 points [1]. The Flames beat Minnesota 2-1 at the Saddledome in October, which The Hockey News reported was the Wild's last regulation loss [1]. Goaltender Dustin Wolf was expected to start for Calgary after a win in San Jose [1].

Former Flames forward Blake Coleman returns to the Saddledome for the second time since joining Minnesota, and was listed on the Wild's third line [1][2]. The Wild's projected goaltenders were Jesper Wallstedt and Calvin Pickard, and the team noted its lineup was subject to change [2].
Calgary's projected lines had Joel Farabee, Mikael Backlund and Matt Coronato together on the top unit, with Zayne Parekh and Simon Nemec among the defencemen [1].

articles.title: More than 60 crashes in eight hours as heavy, wet snow hits Calgary's morning commute
articles.dek: Police counted 16 injury collisions and eight hit-and-runs between midnight and 8 a.m. Wednesday, while Calgary Transit ran its snow detours and trains and buses were delayed.
body: The snowfall forecast on Tuesday arrived overnight, and Calgary drivers paid for it on Wednesday morning, Nov. 18. Calgary police responded to more than 60 collisions between midnight and 8 a.m. [1]. Of those, 16 involved injuries, eight were hit-and-runs and 37 caused no injuries [1].

The most serious crash happened shortly before 7 a.m., when four vehicles collided in the southbound lanes of Deerfoot Trail near Cranston Avenue S.E. [1]. Police said one person was taken to hospital with serious injuries described as life-altering [1]. Global News reported that none of the other collisions that morning were as serious [1]. On Abbot Avenue N.E., a Global News photographer saw three collisions within five minutes [1].

The snow followed several weeks of unseasonably warm November weather [2]. Environment and Climate Change Canada's yellow snowfall warning for Calgary and much of southern Alberta stayed in effect through Wednesday [2][3]. On Tuesday, the agency said 15 to 25 centimetres could fall in some areas, with Calgary expected at the lower end [1]. Another 5 to 10 centimetres was expected on Wednesday [1][3], with final totals of 15 to 30 centimetres across the region before the system eased off Wednesday evening [1]. None of the reports read gave a measured total for the city.

Calgary Transit put all of its snow detours in place, and road conditions delayed buses and trains on both CTrain lines [1]. Global News reported that City crews had a head start on clearing priority routes [1].

Outside the city, Alberta RCMP said roads were in extremely poor condition Wednesday morning, with officers called to collisions across southern Alberta and vehicles stuck in ditches [1]. Several jackknifed semi-trailers closed westbound Highway 1 between Highway 56 and Gleichen, east of Calgary [1].

Calgary Police Service Staff Sgt. Andy Woodward urged drivers to brake early and, if they begin to slide, to steer toward the curb. "Bear in mind your stopping distances," he said [1]. Police also asked drivers to clear snow from their whole vehicle before setting out [1].

articles.title: Council vote count: data centre pause passed 13-2 and heads to a public hearing in March
articles.dek: Calgary council unanimously ordered new zoning rules for data centres and voted 13-2 to send a temporary pause on applications to a public hearing.
body: More details have emerged from Tuesday's council decision on large data centres, including how councillors voted [1]. The motion came from Ward 2 Coun. Jennifer Wyness and was co-signed by Couns. Raj Dhaliwal, Andrew Yule and John Pantazopoulos and Mayor Jeromy Farkas [1].

The part of the motion dealing with oversight passed unanimously [1]. It directs city administration to create a new zoning district that defines data centres, taking different sizes of facility into account, with that work due by March [1]. Administration is also to study the risks, implications and opportunities of data centres, including environmental and economic effects and the impact on regional water, in a report expected by the end of 2027 [1].

A separate amendment dealing with a temporary pause on data centre applications passed 13-2, with Couns. Myke Atkinson and Landon Johnston opposed [1]. That pause is expected to go to a public hearing in March [1]. Wyness said a gap in the land use bylaw has to be closed before a moratorium can be imposed under Alberta's Municipal Government Act [1].

Global News noted that Rocky View County has frozen data centre applications, and that Oakville, Mississauga, Cumberland and Saskatoon have adopted moratoriums [1]. In Calgary, an application to rezone undeveloped land east of 52 Street N.E., north of Redstone, for a large data centre is under review, and the city has asked for studies before a decision is made [1].
The Canadian Coalition for Digital Infrastructure opposes a pause [1]. Farkas, who co-signed the motion, also stressed investment. "Calgary needs to be open for business," he said [1].

articles.title: City picks a site for long-delayed Belvedere police and fire station; land deal expected by 2028
articles.dek: Police have held $32.5 million for an east Calgary district office since 2021 but cannot spend it until the City buys land, which it now expects to do in late 2027 or early 2028.
body: The City of Calgary says it has found land in Belvedere for a long-planned emergency response station in east Calgary, five years after money for a police district office there was set aside [1].

The Calgary Police Service has carried $32.5 million on its books since 2021 for a new Belvedere district office, but cannot spend it because the City has not bought land [1]. The police service's 2027-2030 budget submission says the money came from greenfield development levies, and that the office was planned as part of a shared police and fire site [1]. The police and fire projects are now expected to proceed separately, on different timelines [1]. In late October, Police Chief Katie McLellan confirmed the $32.5 million figure when reporters asked about unspent capital [1].

In an emailed response, the City said the land is meant for the Belvedere Emergency Response Station and a household hazardous waste drop-off, and that negotiations to buy it are underway [1]. The site is south of 17 Avenue S.E. and west of 100 Street S.E., and its land use was approved as part of a developer's outline plan [1]. The City expects to buy the parcel in late 2027 or early 2028, depending on development phasing, servicing and subdivision [1].

Conceptual design is underway, with detailed design and permits expected in 2028 and 2029 and construction to follow [1]. The City said the $32.5 million is not the full cost: the original figure used an assumed rate from an older benchmarking study, and no current estimate is available [1].

Councillors differ on what the station would mean. Ward 9 Coun. Harrison Clark welcomed it for the fast-growing area on the city's eastern edge and said car prowlings and minor thefts are rising there [1]. Ward 10 Coun. Andre Chabot said he doubts a building in the far east would much change police response in either ward, and that faster fire response would be the bigger gain [1]. Chabot also said the developer-levy money should not be moved to other uses, even though it has gone unspent [1].
Council begins deliberations on the City's 2027-2030 budget on Nov. 23, where the police service is seeking a 73 per cent increase in capital spending over four years [1].

articles.title: Two weeks under the water limit: Calgary is halfway through the Bearspaw shutdown
articles.dek: Water use was 482 million litres on Tuesday, and the City says snow and cold are not expected to slow the feeder main connection work.
body: Calgarians used 482 million litres of water on Tuesday, Nov. 17, keeping the city under its 500-million-litre daily limit and marking two weeks in what the City calls the green zone [1]. The City said Wednesday that the city is now halfway through the expected four-week shutdown of the Bearspaw South Feeder Main [1]. The day before, Monday, use was 487 million litres [2].

The limit exists because the City can move only about 500 million litres a day while the feeder main is out of service [1][2]. During the shutdown, the Glenmore plant supplies about 80 per cent of the water and the Bearspaw plant about 20 per cent [2]. Use above the limit would push the city into a red zone, with risks that include not enough water for firefighting, low pressure and a possible boil-water advisory [2].

Work is active at three tie-in locations, and the City said the week's snow and cold are not expected to delay the schedule [1]. Near the Shaganappi Pump Station, welding is complete on installed pipe sections [1]. At 33 Avenue and 89 Street N.W., crews working around the clock are installing the final pipe segments that link the new feeder main and valve chamber to the steel pipe running to the Bearspaw Water Treatment Plant [1]. At 33 Avenue and 83 Street N.W., extra work on an existing pipe has widened the excavation, but the City says that site is on schedule [1]. On Parkdale Boulevard, one of five additional pipe-repair segments is fully installed, and crews are installing and welding the other four [1].

Stage 4 restrictions remain in effect city-wide, and no outdoor water use is allowed, with fines starting at $3,000 [2]. The feeder main has been shut since Nov. 4 for about four weeks [2]. The City says it does not expect restrictions during the commissioning phase in December, but because the old pipe stays in use until the new one is running, restrictions could return on short notice [2]. Neither City page gives a firm end date.

articles.title: Educators raise literacy and university-entry concerns over Alberta's new graduation rules
articles.dek: A University of Alberta education dean and the Alberta Teachers' Association warn that cutting required core courses could leave students less prepared and facing costly upgrades.
body: Five days after the Alberta government released new high school graduation requirements, education leaders are raising concerns about what the changes could mean for literacy and for students who later decide to go to university [1].

Under the rules released Nov. 13, mandatory credits in English language arts, social studies, math and science drop by 15, equal to three fewer core classes at the 20 and 30 levels [1]. Students entering Grade 11 in fall 2029 and Grade 12 in fall 2030 may take half the original number of core classes, while new compulsory physical education-related classes will be required in all three years [1]. Students can still take extra core courses, and those not planning on university may earn their 100 credits with more electives, but must write at least one 30-level diploma exam [1]. Education Minister Demetrios Nicolaides has said the change is about giving students more choice [1].

Jennifer Tupper, dean of education at the University of Alberta, said in a statement that the changes may not be a step in the right direction, and raised questions of equity for students who want post-secondary education [1]. She pointed to the 2025 PISA results, in which Alberta scored highest in Canada in science and reading, but reading scores across Canada fell 17 points from 2022 [1]. The Calgary Board of Education's 2024-25 annual report showed Grade 9 language arts results declining and most Grade 12 language arts and math diploma results below the standard of excellence [1].

Most Alberta and Canadian universities require at least three Grade 12 core courses, and nearly all require English 30-1 [1]. LiveWire Calgary reported that students who change their minds after graduating could need to upgrade two to four courses under the new rules, compared with one or two now for students who skip math or science [1].

Alberta Teachers' Association president Jason Schilling said late last week that the changes risk leaving students less prepared, and asked the province to disclose whose input shaped the proposal [1]. The province has not said whether it will adjust the plan.

body: Two of the week's biggest community events are coming up in Calgary, starting in Kensington on Thursday and ending at Spruce Meadows on Saturday [1][2][3].

The Kensington Business Improvement Area's Kick-Off to Christmas runs Thursday, Nov. 19, from 5:30 p.m., with the tree lighting at 6:20 p.m. [1][2]. Admission costs nothing [1]. Visitors can expect photos with Santa, live duelling pianos, hot chocolate and late shopping, with more than 20 shops staying open, and the evening ends with a 9 p.m. screening of Love Actually at the Plaza Theatre, with tickets through the BIA [1][2]. Environment Canada's forecast for Thursday called for cloud, a 40 per cent chance of flurries and a high of minus 2 [2]. Horse-drawn carriage rides return on Sundays, Nov. 22 and Dec. 20, from noon to 3 p.m. [2]. "Christmas in Kensington is a community celebration," said Gwyneth Midgley, the BIA's executive director [2].

On Saturday, Nov. 21, Cavalry FC plays Atlético Ottawa in the Canadian Premier League Final at 2 p.m. at ATCO Field at Spruce Meadows, 18011 Spruce Meadows Way S.W. [1][3]. It is Cavalry's fourth straight trip to the final [3]. Cavalry reached it by beating FC Supra du Québec 2-0 at home in the second leg of the semifinal, a 3-2 win on aggregate in front of 5,199 fans [3]. Ottawa beat Forge FC 5-4 on aggregate [3].

Cavalry won the regular-season CPL Shield, went 11-0-3 at home and had not lost at ATCO Field since July 2025, according to the Calgary Citizen [3]. articles.dek: Environment Canada expects heavy, wet snow from Tuesday into Wednesday evening across southern Alberta, with travel likely to be difficult through both commutes.
body: Environment Canada issued a yellow-level snowfall warning for Calgary and much of southern Alberta late Tuesday morning, Nov. 17, after an unseasonably warm autumn [1][2].

The warning area stretches from the foothills in the west to the Canada-U.S. border in the south and the Saskatchewan boundary in the east, and reaches north of Calgary about halfway to Red Deer [1]. Forecasters expect general totals of 15 to 20 centimetres, with Calgary at the lower end of that range [1]. Up to 25 centimetres is possible in the foothills, the Cypress Hills and rural areas near Brooks, Medicine Hat and Lethbridge [1]. The Calgary Citizen's morning forecast put the expected window for Calgary at about noon Tuesday through Wednesday evening [4].

The system is moving north and east through the day. Areas near the Saskatchewan border were expected to see rain first, turning to heavy snow Tuesday evening, before the snow tapers off Wednesday evening as the system moves into Saskatchewan [1]. Environment and Climate Change Canada also issued special weather statements for parts of central Alberta, where 5 to 10 centimetres is expected around Red Deer [1][2].

Environment Canada said travel will likely be challenging and could significantly affect the Tuesday evening rush hour, and advised drivers to prepare for conditions that change quickly [1]. Calgarians were also being encouraged to drive with care ahead of the snowfall [3].

Temperatures are expected to hover near the freezing mark, with a forecast high of 1 C on Tuesday and Wednesday and a high of minus 1 C on Thursday, according to the Calgary Citizen's daily forecast [4]. The snow arrives while Stage 4 outdoor water restrictions remain in effect in the city [4].

articles.title: Council moves ahead on data centre rules, with bylaw options due by March 2027
articles.dek: Calgary city council directed staff to prepare land-use changes that could allow a moratorium on large data centres and to study their effects on water, power and noise.
body: Calgary city council has agreed to move forward with work on rules for large-scale data centres, following a committee recommendation earlier this month that came in response to a large data centre land-use application in the city's far northeast [1].

Council directed city administration to prepare options for changes to the Land Use Bylaw that could allow a moratorium on development applications for new and emerging sectors [1]. Administration was also told to bring back possible bylaw amendments to govern the buildings themselves, and to research how large data centres affect water, electricity and noise [1]. The report did not give a vote count [1].

Administration is expected to report back on the bylaw changes, including moratorium powers and any data-centre-specific updates, by March 2027 [1]. The research on impacts is expected in the fourth quarter of 2027 [1].

Ward 2 Coun. Jennifer Wyness, who led the push for data centre guidelines, said the city's bylaws have a gap because they do not specifically provide for a moratorium, and noted that other Alberta municipalities have adopted one [1]. She also raised concern that, according to administration, there is industrial land already inside city limits where a data centre would not need a land-use change [1]. Administration said its development permit process is robust enough to identify concerns [1].

Ward 13 Coun. Dan McLean said he wants strong safeguards around construction, while Ward 14 Coun. Landon Johnston said he wants the facts right and no bias toward a particular outcome [1]. Mayor Jeromy Farkas said the city has a vacuum when it comes to mega-scale data centres and called for strict rules on noise, water and electricity [1].

Provincial guidance covers data centres of 75 megawatts or more and gives priority to projects that generate their own power [1]. The Alberta Utilities Commission recently rejected a power generation site for a proposed data centre near Olds [1].

articles.dek: The $19-million project took 18 months and turned a two-lane stretch used by more than 24,000 drivers a day into a six-lane arterial.
body: The City of Calgary says the widening of Country Hills Boulevard N.E. between Barlow Trail and 36 Street N.E. is complete, and the roughly 800-metre stretch is now fully open as a six-lane arterial road [1][2]. It was previously two lanes [1][2].

The project cost $19 million and took 18 months of construction, and the City said it was finished on time and on budget [1][2]. More than 24,000 drivers use the corridor each day, and the City kept traffic moving during the work on a paved and lit temporary detour [1].

Crews removed old overhead power and communication lines and poles and moved them into new underground ducts [1][2]. They installed new deep utilities, including 700 metres of new water feeder main for a future connection, upgraded intersections and added new traffic signals [1]. The finished road has a regional pathway on the south side and a sidewalk on the north side [1][2].

The release quoted Mayor Jeromy Farkas, Ward 5 Coun. Raj Dhaliwal and Ryan Atkinson, the City's director of public spaces delivery [1][2]. The City pointed to the proposed Airport Trail N.E. twinning project as an example of further planned work in the area [1][2].

articles.title: City proposes $3.1 million to protect bridges after encampment fires cost $2.7 million in repairs
articles.dek: Five major fires under Calgary bridges since 2021 led to about $2.688 million in repairs, and the proposed budget would fund fencing, lighting and fire-retardant coatings.
body: Five major fires at encampments under Calgary bridges since 2021 have cost the city about $2.688 million in repairs, according to figures reported ahead of budget deliberations [1].

The proposed 2027-2030 budget includes $3.1 million in capital funding for physical deterrents under some bridges, a program that was not funded in the 2023-2026 budget [1]. The money would be spent in 2027 and 2028, with nothing set aside for 2029 or 2030 [1].

The measures under consideration include heavy-duty perimeter fencing, high-visibility lighting and fire-retardant coatings, and placing rock riprap or changing slopes was also mentioned [1]. About 50 bridges are candidate sites, and the city would finalize and rank the list if the funding is approved [1]. The city said the measures' effectiveness cannot be guaranteed [1].

Ward 9 Coun. Harrison Clark questioned the value of the lighting and said fire-retardant coatings would be the most suitable fix if the goal is to prevent bridge fires [1]. Ward 8 Coun. Nathan Schmidt said the spending may be needed now but addresses symptoms, and pointed to housing, a delayed 60-unit HomeSpace housing site and the size of the city's encampment team [1].
Council has not voted on the item. Budget deliberations begin Nov. 23 [1], and council will hear from members of the public that day, with registration required to speak [2].

articles.title: Water use stays under the limit for a 13th straight day as Bearspaw connection work stays on schedule
articles.dek: Calgarians used 487 million litres on Monday, and the City says crews are welding replacement pipe at several sites while Stage 4 restrictions continue.
body: Calgary's water use came in at 487 million litres on Monday, Nov. 16, keeping the city in the green zone below its 500-million-litre daily limit for a 13th day in a row [1][2]. Use was 474 million litres on Saturday and 490 million on Sunday over Grey Cup weekend [4].

The City says use above 500 million litres a day puts it in a red zone, with risks that include not enough water for firefighting, low pressure, a possible boil water advisory and failure of the treatment plants or system [1]. During the shutdown, the two plants can supply 500 million litres a day, with the Glenmore plant serving about 80 per cent of the city and region [3].

In its Tuesday update, the City said work on connecting the new Bearspaw South Feeder Main is on schedule [1]. Tie-in work is underway at the Shaganappi Pump Station, where welding is complete on installed pipe sections [1]. At 33 Avenue and 89 Street N.W., crews are installing the final pipe segments that link the new feeder main and valve chamber to the steel pipe running to the Bearspaw Water Treatment Plant, with construction around the clock until it is done [1]. Excavation is underway at 33 Avenue and 83 Street N.W., and replacement pipe is being welded at five locations along Parkdale Boulevard [1].

Stage 4 restrictions, in effect since Nov. 4, ban most outdoor water use, with fines starting at $3,000 [3]. The City has said the feeder main would be out of service for about four weeks, with commissioning of the new pipe planned for December [3].

articles.dek: Drivers carrying a child in an improperly secured seat could be fined up to $211.
body: Calgary police are running check stops around the city throughout November to make sure children's car seats are properly installed and secured [1][2].

Drivers with a child in a seat that is not properly secured could face a fine of up to $211, police said in a release issued Monday, Nov. 16 [1][2]. The checks are taking place at locations across the city rather than in a single area, and will continue until the end of the month [1][2].

Police listed several common mistakes: chest clips placed too low, internal harness straps that are too loose, seats that are not tethered, and seats that are installed loosely [1]. Police pointed parents and caregivers to Alberta's car seat guidelines and to provincial health information on rear-facing, forward-facing and booster seats [1]. Those resources include separate pages on myhealth.alberta.ca for rear-facing seats, forward-facing seats and booster seats [1].

The check stops are part of the City's Vision Zero road safety campaign, and more information on that program is posted at calgary.ca/VisionZero [1]. The Calgary Citizen also highlighted the check stops in its Tuesday morning newsletter [2].

articles.title: Ken Newans, longtime voice of Calgary sports and the Stampeders, dies at 95
articles.dek: The former CFCN sports director covered 30 Grey Cups and called Stampeders games, and tributes came in over Grey Cup weekend in Calgary.
body: Ken Newans, a Calgary sports broadcaster whose career spanned decades, died on Saturday, Nov. 14, at the age of 95 [1][2].

Newans was sports director at CFCN in Calgary in the 1970s and was the Calgary Stampeders' play-by-play voice as well as their public address announcer [1]. He brought Calgarians sports on CFCN for almost three decades, covered 30 Grey Cups and seven Olympic Games, and called Stampeders games for 12 seasons [2].

He was also the public address voice of University of Calgary Dinos football for 27 seasons [1][2]. When the Dinos won the 1995 Vanier Cup, he was the only person outside the team to receive a championship ring [2]. He was the only person to win the Fred Sgambati Award twice for coverage of Canadian university sport, and received the University of Calgary athletics department's Distinguished Service Award in 1992 [1].

Newans was inducted into the CFL reporters' Hall of Fame in 1991 and into the Alberta Sports Hall of Fame in 2011 as a multisport builder, and is also a member of the Canadian Boxing Hall of Fame [1].

Tributes came in as Calgary hosted the 113th Grey Cup on Sunday [1]. The Stampeders posted a tribute on social media, and broadcasters including longtime Stampeders play-by-play announcer Mark Stephen and CTV Calgary sports anchor Glenn Campbell spoke of him as a mentor and supporter [1]. Campbell said Newans "took a chance on me and was my mentor" [1].

articles.title: Edmonton Elks beat Montreal 37-30 to win the 113th Grey Cup at McMahon Stadium
articles.dek: Calgary's sixth Grey Cup ended with Edmonton's first championship since 2015, and Tourism Calgary estimates the week brought about $50 million in economic activity.
body: The Edmonton Elks won the 113th Grey Cup on Sunday, Nov. 15, defeating the Montreal Alouettes 37-30 at McMahon Stadium in Calgary [1][2]. It is the club's 15th Grey Cup since it was founded in 1949 and its first since 2015, when the team, then called the Eskimos, beat Ottawa 26-20 [1].

Quarterback Cody Fajardo was named the game's most valuable player, his second Grey Cup MVP award in four years [2]. He threw for 199 yards with two touchdown passes and one interception, and ran for 45 yards and two more touchdowns [2]. Montreal had released Fajardo a year after he led the Alouettes to the 2023 championship [1]. Rookie receiver Joshua Cephus caught two touchdown passes, including the go-ahead score in the third quarter, and running back Justin Rankin ran for 85 yards [2].

The game swung back and forth. Edmonton led 21-17 at halftime and 31-24 going into the fourth quarter [3]. Montreal quarterback Davis Alexander, the league's most outstanding player this season, completed 21 of 36 passes for 226 yards and a touchdown but hurt his shoulder late in the third quarter [2]. Alouettes receiver Tyson Philpot was named the game's most valuable Canadian, the first player from the losing side to win the award since 2017 [2]. Montreal kicked its final field goal with five seconds left [2].

Both teams had finished first in their divisions. Edmonton went 13-5 and beat the B.C. Lions 28-16 in the West final, while Montreal went 14-4 and beat the Winnipeg Blue Bombers 33-23 in the East final [1]. The Elks' turnaround began in 2024, when the team was sold to the late Larry Thompson and his wife, Deb Thompson [1][2].

Pre-game entertainment included the James Barker Band and Blue Rodeo, with Sarah McLachlan singing the anthem, and Riley Green performed at halftime [3]. The temperature at kickoff was about 14 degrees [3]. It was Calgary's sixth time hosting the Grey Cup, after 2019, and the Calgary Journal noted it could be the last one played at McMahon Stadium [3].

Tourism Calgary estimates the Grey Cup festivities brought about $50 million in economic activity to the city [4]. Steve Sommerfeld chaired the Calgary Grey Cup Committee, which opened the festival week on Thursday, Nov. 12 [4]. Elks head coach Mark Kilam summed up his team after the win: "We're not a sexy team." [2]

articles.title: Water use rose to 490 million litres on Grey Cup Sunday but stayed under the limit
articles.dek: Calgary has now stayed under its 500-million-litre daily target for 12 straight days as Bearspaw South feeder main tie-in work passes the halfway mark.
body: Calgarians used 490 million litres of water on Sunday, Nov. 15, the day of the Grey Cup, city officials said Monday [1][2][3]. That was up from 477 million litres on Saturday but still under the 500-million-litre daily target set while the Bearspaw South feeder main is out of service [2]. CTV News reported the Sunday figure as a 16-million-litre rise over the day before, which does not match the Saturday figure the city gave the Calgary Herald [3][2].

The city has stayed in the green zone every day for 12 days, since temporary Stage 4 water restrictions took effect on Nov. 4 [2]. Mayor Jeromy Farkas said use stayed below typical levels even with about 35,000 visitors in town for the game [1]. "We're bringing the green zone to the end zone," Farkas said [2].

Farkas said the project is nearly halfway complete [2]. The Canadian Press described the city as about halfway through roughly three weeks of restrictions [1]. The Stage 4 rules stay in place until the Bearspaw South feeder main is back in service; that line carries about 60 per cent of Calgary's treated water [2]. No end date has been announced [2].

Crews are joining the new steel pipe to the existing feeder main at three sites: the Shaganappi Pump Station near Edworthy Park, where pipe sections were placed and welded over the weekend; 33 Avenue and 89 Street N.W., where excavation is finished and the last pipe pieces are going in; and 83 Street N.W., where digging is under way [2].

Separate work on the 1,500-millimetre feeder main between the Shaganappi and Memorial pump stations has been postponed at one of six planned sites, which lies under a park, until next year because of a leaky valve; that work does not need restrictions [2]. A repair to a leak on the Edgemont feeder main is also under way, and residents of Edgemont, the Hamptons, Citadel, Hawkwood and Arbour Lake may see temporary low water pressure, though the water remains safe to drink [2].
The restrictions are meant to keep the water treatment plant from being strained and to keep enough water on hand for firefighting [1].

articles.title: Alberta tables bill to put new electoral map into law, including hybrid Calgary divisions
articles.dek: The legislation would raise the number of seats from 87 to 91 before the October 2027 election; the Opposition NDP says it will challenge the map in court.
body: The Alberta government on Monday, Nov. 16, tabled legislation to put new electoral division boundaries into law ahead of the next provincial general election, scheduled for Oct. 18, 2027 [1][2]. The bill's number and name were not given in the reports.

The new map would raise the number of seats in the legislature from 87 to 91, as recommended in an advisory panel report published earlier in November [1]. It includes hybrid electoral divisions that combine some urban voters in Calgary and Lethbridge with surrounding rural areas [1]. In Lethbridge, the city's two current urban divisions would become four: one entirely urban and three hybrids, some of them reaching the U.S. border [1]. The reports did not say how many Calgary divisions would change.

The map follows a change of course earlier this year. Premier Danielle Smith's government voted down the proposals of the public electoral boundaries commission, then appointed a committee to oversee a new advisory panel with a chair appointed by the governing United Conservative Party [1]. UCP members were unanimous in a symbolic vote earlier this month endorsing the changes [1].

Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said the new divisions dilute urban votes to benefit the UCP and called the plan "very likely unconstitutional" [1]. He said the party will challenge the law in court but must wait until it receives royal assent before filing [1].

The government denies trying to tilt the 2027 election. It says the map improves effective representation and points out that hybrid divisions already exist elsewhere in Alberta [1]. Justice Minister Mickey Amery described hybrid divisions as the way of the future and dismissed the possible court challenge as sour grapes [1].
The bill must pass the legislature and receive royal assent before it takes effect [1][2].

articles.title: Thirty-five people killed in crashes on Calgary roads so far in 2026, police say
articles.dek: Police count 29 fatal collisions this year, a pace that would top 2025, which was already the deadliest year in a decade by mid-November.
body: Calgary police say 29 fatal collisions on city roads so far in 2026 have killed 35 people, CTV News reported on Monday, Nov. 16 [1]. The report says this year's death toll is on pace to surpass 2025 [1]. Police did not give a full-year 2025 figure in the material available.

Last year was already a high-water mark. In a joint release on Nov. 14, 2025, the Calgary Police Service and the City of Calgary said there had been 31 fatal collisions with 31 deaths to that point in 2025, a 10-year high [2]. More than 2,500 collisions that year had injured drivers, passengers, pedestrians, cyclists or motorcyclists [2].

The 2025 release broke down the fatal crashes to that date. Speed was a factor in 12 of the 31, three were hit-and-runs, and at least four involved drugs or alcohol, with some toxicology results still pending [2]. Twenty, or about 65 per cent, involved a pedestrian, motorcyclist or cyclist [2].
Over the past decade, the number of fatal collisions in Calgary has ranged from 11 in 2017 to 29 in 2024, according to the city's figures [2]. Injury collisions peaked at 2,903 in 2024 [2].

The city's Safer Mobility Plan follows a Vision Zero approach that aims to eliminate traffic deaths and major injuries [2]. Pat Grisak, the city's senior leader of traffic management, said at the time: "One death on our roads is too many." [2] The World Day of Remembrance for Road Traffic Victims is marked on the third Sunday of November each year, and the 2025 release was issued ahead of that day [2].
A photo with the CTV report shows fire crews at a deadly three-vehicle crash on Stoney Trail in southwest Calgary on Aug. 2, 2026 [1].

articles.title: Trial hears of handgun drawn in Martindale temple parking lot during 2024 confrontation
articles.dek: Two men face threat and firearms charges; a witness told a Calgary court one of them pulled a gun from his waistband during an argument.
body: The Calgary Court of Justice is hearing the trial of two men accused of threatening a man outside a Sikh temple in the northeast community of Martindale in September 2024, the Calgary Herald reported on Monday, Nov. 16 [1]. None of the allegations has been proven in court.

Gursewak Singh, 34, and Sukhpreet Singh, 24, each face a charge of uttering threats dated Sept. 24, 2024, along with four firearms-related charges [1]. Gursewak Singh faces five further counts, including pointing a firearm, possessing a stolen firearm and possessing opium [1]. The case is being heard by Justice Judith Shriar [1].

The witness, whose home had been shot at days earlier, testified that he had just left a meeting at the Dashmesh Cultural Centre when he was approached in the parking lot [1]. He said he and Gursewak Singh had a loud argument, during which he asked whether Gursewak Singh was behind the shooting at his home and a threatening phone call [1]. The witness told the court Gursewak Singh pulled a gun from his waistband and waved it toward the group [1]. Cellphone videos shown in court, recorded in Punjabi, show a silver handgun [1].

Asked by Crown prosecutor Matt Dalidowicz how he felt, the witness said anybody would have been scared [1]. In the Crown's opening, the court heard that police found a loaded .357 revolver in Gursewak Singh's waistband and a loaded 9mm pistol in an inside jacket pocket worn by Sukhpreet Singh [1]. The witness said the gun was no longer in Gursewak Singh's hand when police arrived [1].

Gursewak Singh is also scheduled to stand trial next week on allegations related to the Sept. 19, 2024 shooting at the witness's home and an extortion allegation [1]. The accused have not been convicted of any offence.

articles.title: Calgary hosts the 113th Grey Cup as Montreal and Edmonton meet at McMahon Stadium
articles.dek: The Alouettes and Elks play for the CFL championship Sunday evening in Calgary, the city's sixth time hosting the game and its first since 2019.
body: The Montreal Alouettes and the Edmonton Elks meet in the 113th Grey Cup on Sunday, Nov. 15, at McMahon Stadium in northwest Calgary, with kickoff set for 5 p.m. Alberta time and gates opening at 3 p.m. [2][3]. It is the sixth time Calgary has hosted the Canadian Football League championship and the first since 2019 [3].

Both teams finished first in their divisions. Montreal went 14-4 and beat the Winnipeg Blue Bombers 33-23 in the East final, while Edmonton went 13-5 and beat the B.C. Lions 28-16 in the West final [1]. The two clubs split their regular-season meetings: Edmonton won 32-29 in overtime on June 20, and Montreal won 48-30 on Aug. 8 [1].

The game is the 12th Grey Cup meeting between the two franchises, and Edmonton has won eight of the first 11 [2]. Edmonton is making its first Grey Cup appearance since 2015, when it beat Ottawa 26-20 in Winnipeg [1]. Montreal lost last year's final 25-17 to Saskatchewan [1].

Elks quarterback Cody Fajardo faces his former team; he was the most valuable player of the 2023 Grey Cup while playing for Montreal [1]. Alouettes quarterback Davis Alexander was named the league's Most Outstanding Player this season [2]. Montreal receiver Tyson Philpot, named Most Outstanding Canadian, set Canadian single-season records with 124 catches and 1,809 receiving yards, and his twin brother Jalen plays for the Calgary Stampeders [3]. Montreal opened as a narrow betting favourite [3].

Sarah McLachlan is scheduled to sing the anthem and country singer Riley Green to perform at halftime, with the James Barker Band on the kickoff show [2][3]. The game airs on TSN and CTV in English and RDS in French, and streams on Crave and TSN's platforms [2].

For fans heading to the stadium, organizers pointed to the CTrain Red Line to Banff Trail Station [2]. University Drive N.W. is closed between 16 Avenue and 24 Avenue from 11 a.m. to 11 p.m., except for marked taxis, rideshare and accredited vehicles, and parts of 23 Avenue and Banff Trail N.W. are also closed [2]. A public pickup spot is on 24 Street N.W., across Crowchild Trail from the stadium [2]. A family tailgate party in the stadium's east parking lot runs from 1 to 5 p.m. at no charge [2][3].

The game wraps up a week-long festival at Stampede Park that began Wednesday and included street festivals, a family zone at the BMO Centre and nightly drone shows [3]. The result was not yet known when this edition was published.

An earlier Herald report described the case as a suspicious death and said the cause of death had not yet been determined, while the later police release calls it a fatal shooting [1][2]. body: Calgary and the communities it supplies used 474 million litres of water on Saturday, Nov. 14, keeping daily use in the city's green zone below the 500-million-litre limit on the first full day of Grey Cup weekend visitors, according to the City's update on Sunday [1].

The 500-million-litre figure is roughly what the Glenmore and Bearspaw treatment plants can supply together while the Bearspaw South Feeder Main is shut down, the City says [1]. During the shutdown, Glenmore is supplying about 80 per cent of the city's water and Bearspaw about 20 per cent [1].

Saturday's total was lower than the figures reported in the first days of the restrictions. Global News reported use of 482 million litres on Friday, Nov. 6, 483 million on Saturday, Nov. 7, and 487 million on Sunday, Nov. 8 [2].

Stage 4 outdoor restrictions have been in effect city-wide since Nov. 4, meaning no outdoor water use is allowed, and fines start at $3,000 [1]. The City continues to ask residents to cut indoor use as well [1]. The old pipe was shut down for about four weeks so the new feeder main can be connected, and the City says it does not expect restrictions during commissioning of the new pipe in December, though it warns they could be reintroduced at any time before then [1].

Global News reported earlier that crews were moving to round-the-clock work at the 89 Street N.W. connection site for about two weeks starting Nov. 12, and that the City expected restrictions to last at least three and a half weeks from Nov. 9 [2]. articles.title: Grey Cup Sunday: Calgary Transit points fans to the Red Line and a North Pointe shuttle
articles.dek: With no public parking at McMahon Stadium for Sunday's 113th Grey Cup, the city's transit guide sends fans to Banff Trail Station and an express shuttle from North Pointe.
body: Football fans heading to the 113th Grey Cup at McMahon Stadium on Sunday, Nov. 15, are being steered onto transit. Calgary Transit's game-day guide directs riders to the Red Line CTrain and Banff Trail Station, a short walk from the stadium, and warns that the station can be very busy, so riders should arrive early [1]. The guide says extra trains will be added as needed [1].
There is no public parking at McMahon on game day, and gates open at 3 p.m. [2]. The championship game between the Edmonton Elks and the Montreal Alouettes kicks off at 5 p.m. Calgary time [3].

A Grey Cup Express Shuttle will run between North Pointe Terminal and the stadium's west entrance [1]. Buses leave North Pointe Stop A every 30 minutes starting at 12:30 p.m., with the last pre-game bus at 4 p.m.; after the game, return shuttles run as needed [1]. Regular bus routes 9, 19, 20, 40, 90, 91, 104 and MAX Orange also serve the area, and Route 19 stops at the west entrance [1].

Banff Trail Station is outside the downtown zone where CTrain rides cost nothing, so riders need a fare [1]. The guide lists an adult cash fare of $4 and a Weekend Group 1-Day Pass for up to five people at $18; children 12 and under ride at no charge [1].

The guide flags several other points [1]. Many routes run reduced Sunday service. The walk from Banff Trail crosses a long pedestrian bridge over Crowchild Trail, which some riders may find difficult. And the real-time arrival system is down for maintenance, so live arrival times may be inaccurate. Extended late-night CTrain service until 2 a.m. was scheduled only for Nov. 12 to 14, not for game day itself [1].

The city expects up to 350,000 people to take part in Grey Cup events over the week, including about 35,000 visitors from across Canada [3]. The Grey Cup Festival at Stampede Park runs through Saturday night at the BMO Centre and Lot 3, from 11 a.m. to 9 p.m., with a drone show at 8:45 p.m. [2].

articles.title: Proposed budget would raise youth arena ice rates sharply in 2027, alarming minor hockey
articles.dek: Fee schedules in the city's proposed 2027-2030 budget would lift minor non-prime ice from $82.30 to $133.33 an hour, and Hockey Calgary says it was not consulted.
body: Calgary's proposed 2027-2030 budget includes steep increases to the hourly rates that minor and youth groups pay to rent city arena ice [1]. The fee schedules, found on page 268 of the budget document, have not been approved by council [1].

Under the proposal, minor non-prime ice in July and August would rise from $82.30 an hour to $133.33 in 2027 and reach $141.76 an hour by 2030 [1]. Minor and youth prime-time ice would go from $230.30 an hour to $270.83 in 2027 and later to $287.97 [1]. Those figures work out to roughly a 62 per cent jump for non-prime ice and about 18 per cent for prime time in the first year.

Hockey Calgary executive director Kevin Kobelka said his organization was neither informed nor consulted [1]. He said ice makes up 65 to 70 per cent of program costs and estimated that average program fees would have to rise 15 to 20 per cent to absorb the change [1]. He questioned why adult ice fees rose only slightly, why public skating was not asked to share the increase, and why turf and other recreation fees rise only a few per cent, and he warned that the cost could push some families out of the sport [1]. He said the increase is "really targeted at minor hockey, ringette, and figure skating" [1].

The city says some ice rates have stayed below market after years of limited increases and periods when fees were held flat, and that the changes take into account inflation, customer demand, the cost of delivering the service and rates relative to the market [1]. For comparison, youth ice at WinSport costs $176 an hour non-prime and $276.36 prime, while YMCA arenas charge $175 non-prime and $296 prime [1].

At least two councillors have raised objections [1]. Ward 10 Coun. Andre Chabot said the city owns its facilities so it can offer lower prices than the private sector, and Ward 8 Coun. Nathan Schmidt warned against creating barriers to youth sports at a time of affordability concerns and projected tax increases [1].
Council's budget deliberations begin Nov. 23, when the fee schedules can still be changed [1].

articles.title: Water use holds under target as Edgemont leak repair adds a second job in the northwest
articles.dek: Calgary used 477 million litres on Nov. 12, and a separate water main repair in Edgemont may lower water pressure in five northwest communities for up to 10 days.
body: Calgary and the neighbouring communities it supplies used 477 million litres of water on Thursday, Nov. 12, staying below the 500-million-litre daily target that keeps the system in what the city calls the green zone [1][2]. Use was 473 million litres on Nov. 10 and 475 million on Nov. 11 [3].

New since the last update, the city says a separate repair to a leaking water main in Edgemont began on Nov. 13 and should take seven to 10 days [1]. Residents of Edgemont, Hamptons, Citadel, Hawkwood and Arbour Lake may notice lower water pressure during that time, but the city says the water remains safe to drink [1].

Stage 4 outdoor water restrictions have been in force city-wide since Nov. 4, when the Bearspaw South Feeder Main was shut down for about four weeks so the new pipe can be connected; indoor conservation is also requested [2]. The city warns that use above 500 million litres could mean low supply for firefighting, low pressure, a possible boil-water advisory or a treatment plant failure [2]. The target matters because the city relies mainly on a single treatment plant during the shutdown [1].

So far, use has averaged 483 million litres a day, compared with 505 million a day over the same Nov. 4 to 11 period in 2025, when no restrictions were in place [4]. About a week of the four-week shutdown was complete as of Nov. 12, and water officials said the work was on schedule [4].

On the work sites, the city's Nov. 13 update says new pipe is in and welding has begun at the Shaganappi Pump Station, and crews are installing a new valve at 33 Avenue and 89 Street N.W. [1]. The city's update says round-the-clock work at that site is to start on the evening of Sunday, Nov. 15, and continue for about two weeks until the connection is complete; an earlier city update on Nov. 12 had pointed to Saturday [1][3]. Asphalt removal at 83 Street N.W. began Nov. 13, with single-lane alternating traffic and no westbound turns onto 33 Avenue N.W. from 83 Street [1]. Repairs on the 1,500-millimetre feeder main along Parkdale Boulevard and Memorial Drive N.W. are on schedule [1].

Water utility chief operating officer Michael Thompson said staying in the green zone gives the system a buffer for Grey Cup crowds [1]. The city expects restrictions to last until around the end of November, with commissioning of the new pipe planned for December [2].

articles.title: Calgary man charged after OPP seize more than 100 kilograms of suspected cocaine near Thunder Bay
articles.dek: Ontario Provincial Police say a traffic stop on Highway 11/17 turned up drugs with an estimated street value of $11.5 million.
body: A 32-year-old Calgary man faces drug trafficking charges after Ontario Provincial Police seized more than 100 kilograms of suspected cocaine during a traffic stop in northwestern Ontario [1][2].

Police say officers stopped a vehicle on Highway 11/17 near the Loon Lake area in Shuniah, near Thunder Bay, at about 3:15 p.m. Eastern time on Wednesday, Nov. 11 [1]. The OPP announced the seizure in a news release on Nov. 13 and estimated the street value of the drugs at $11.5 million [1].

The Calgary Herald identified the accused as Varinder Hundal, 32, of Calgary [2]. He is charged with trafficking a Schedule 1 substance and possession of cocaine for the purpose of trafficking [1][2]. OPP spokesperson Eric McCrea spoke to CTV News about the case, though the text of the CTV report did not name the accused [1]. The Herald's account, based on the OPP release, describes officers seizing more than 100 kilograms of suspected cocaine from the vehicle [2].

The accused is to appear in the Ontario Court of Justice in Thunder Bay on a date that has not yet been set [1]. The charges have not been proven in court. No further details about the vehicle, its route or any other suspects were included in the reports [1][2].

articles.title: Pubs and hotels say water rules will not dry up Grey Cup weekend
articles.dek: Brewers cut water use and hotel restaurants serve water on request as the city prepares for up to 350,000 Grey Cup fans under Stage 4 restrictions.
body: Calgary businesses expecting Grey Cup crowds say the city's water restrictions should not keep them from serving customers [1]. The city expects up to 350,000 fans over the festival, including about 35,000 visitors from across Canada, along with about 6,000 additional hotel room nights booked [1].

City officials do not expect trouble staying under the 500-million-litre daily limit during Grey Cup weekend, the report says [1]. Residents are being asked to cut water use until around the end of November while the Bearspaw South Feeder Main is reconnected, the fifth time Calgary has faced restrictions because of problems with the pipe [1].

At Bottlescrew Bill's Pub, co-owner Geoff Allan said the pub expects to have enough product on hand [1]. Head brewer Melissa Pawlak said brewing happens weeks in advance, and the pub has halved its usual brewing water use of about 2,000 litres by shutting down a less water-efficient system [1]. Allan said, "we shouldn't be running out of our own product" [1].

Kampus Brewing, located near McMahon Stadium, said it is well stocked [1]. At the Hyatt Regency Calgary, general manager John O'Connell said guests co-operate once they are told about the restrictions, and the hotel restaurant serves water only on request [1].
Earlier rounds of restrictions tied to the feeder main came before the 2024 Calgary Stampede and over New Year's Eve 2025 [1]. The 113th Grey Cup is played at McMahon Stadium on Sunday, Nov. 15 [1].

articles.title: Could this be McMahon's last Grey Cup? Options for a new Calgary football stadium remain open
articles.dek: The Stampede, the city and the University of Calgary are each studying pieces of the puzzle as the 66-year-old stadium hosts Sunday's championship.
body: As McMahon Stadium hosts the 113th Grey Cup on Sunday, Nov. 15, the 66-year-old venue's future is under discussion, with some in the city asking whether this will be the last Grey Cup played there [1].

Several options are being studied, though none has been chosen [1]. The Calgary Stampede has hired a firm to look at adapting the 17,000-seat GMC Stadium grandstand for football and possibly soccer, and expects an answer by summer 2027 [1]. The City of Calgary is running a feasibility study on major sports and event infrastructure, which StadiumDB puts at about $875,000 [1][3]. The University of Calgary wants a 5,000-seat stadium on campus and has raised about $23 million toward it [1].

In the meantime, seats salvaged from the Scotiabank Saddledome could serve as a stopgap, because replacement parts for McMahon's seats are no longer available [1]. The McMahon Stadium Society wants a new building ready for the 2033 season, since the stadium's new turf has an eight-year lifespan [1]. Society chair Steve Allan said, "It's time for a new building" [1].

Nearly $1 million went into water and sewer repairs at the stadium ahead of this Grey Cup, according to StadiumDB [3]. By comparison, the new Scotia Place arena, where the Flames move next year, cost $1.22 billion [1]. Mayor Jeromy Farkas has said any public money for a stadium must be economically justified [3].

On CTV's Alberta Primetime on Nov. 13, political scientist Duane Bratt and LiveWire Calgary founder Darren Krause discussed the stadium's future, with the program describing the path to a new football stadium as complicated [2].

articles.title: Alberta overhauls high school graduation rules, giving students more course choice from 2028
articles.dek: The province will cut core credit requirements and drop mandatory senior math and science, while making physical education and a wellness and financial literacy course required in every high school year.
body: The Alberta government announced on Friday, Nov. 13, that it is changing what students must take to graduate from high school, a shift that will affect every Calgary high school once it takes effect in 2028 [1][2].

Students will still need 100 credits to graduate, but optional courses will be able to make up as many as 53 of those credits, up from 44 under the current rules [1]. Core credit requirements fall from 56 to 47 for students who start high school in 2028 [2].

In Grades 11 and 12, students will need 10 credits in English language arts, social studies or a combination of the two, rather than 10 credits in each [1]. They will need five credits in math or science, rather than five in each [1]. The Canadian Press reported that students will need only one senior English or social studies course and that senior math and science courses will no longer be required [2].

English, social studies, math and science will remain mandatory in Grade 10 [1]. Physical education and wellness will expand across Grades 10 to 12, and a wellness and financial literacy course will be required in all three years of high school [1][2]. Students must also write at least one diploma exam, in English language arts, social studies, math or science [1].
The changes will roll out in stages: Grade 10 students in fall 2028, Grade 11 students in 2029 and Grade 12 students in 2030 [1].
Education and Childcare Minister Demetrios Nicolaides said the province is not lowering the bar. "More flexibility does not mean lower expectations," he said [2].

The Alberta Teachers' Association disagreed with the approach. Its president, Jason Schilling, said Grade 12 English language arts and social studies are essential and that education partners were not meaningfully consulted on the proposal [1]. Bradey Thompson, principal and co-founder of Fusion Collegiate, said the current rules have served many students well but that students take different paths after high school [1].
The announcement does not change requirements for students already in high school, since the first group affected is students entering Grade 10 in fall 2028 [1][2].

articles.title: Ottawa announces about $17 million in tariff relief for 18 Calgary-area businesses
articles.dek: A federal minister also promoted a new tax deduction for business investment at an event in southeast Calgary on Friday.
body: Eighteen Calgary-area businesses will share more than $17 million in federal money meant to help them cope with the effects of U.S. tariffs, the Government of Canada announced on Friday, Nov. 13 [1][2].

Eleanor Olszewski, the federal Minister of Emergency Management and Community Resilience and the minister responsible for Prairies Economic Development Canada, made the announcement at a news conference in an industrial park in southeast Calgary [1][2]. The event was held at the Shepard Industrial Park plant of Tech Wood Building Components [2].

The money comes from the Regional Tariff Response Initiative, a $3.45-billion federal program [1]. Each business receives up to $1 million as a non-repayable contribution [1]. The federal release lists the businesses as working in construction, advanced manufacturing, agriculture and health sciences, and puts the Prairie total administered by the agency at $17.6 million [1].

Three recipients were described in Calgary Herald coverage. Big Rock Brewery is receiving $850,000 to modernize its manufacturing, increase production, expand co-packaging and develop new drinks and packaging formats [2]. Fitness equipment maker Bells of Steel is receiving $1 million to improve its warehouse and speed up automation, and Tech Wood Building Components is receiving $1 million to expand and modernize its plant and add automation [2]. Olszewski said the funding will support 190 jobs in Calgary [2].

The minister also promoted the Productivity Mega Deduction, which the federal release says lowers the marginal effective tax rate on new business investment from 13 per cent to 6.4 per cent [1]. The Herald reported that it widens the types of assets that qualify, from about 15 per cent of assets to more than 65 per cent, covering items such as software, computer equipment, vehicles, pipelines and research and development [2]. Olszewski said the change will generate about $2.2 billion a year in economic activity over the next decade [2].
The sources describe the deduction differently: the federal release ties it to Budget 2026, while the Herald story calls it part of the recently tabled 2027 budget [1][2].

"Alberta businesses have always found ways to get things done," Olszewski said in the release [1]. The tariff initiative is part of a $7.5-billion federal package for workers and businesses affected by U.S. tariffs [1].

articles.title: Province proposes 10-year royalty break to spur new oilsands projects
articles.dek: The voluntary Oil Sands Growth Program would charge new projects and expansions a royalty starting at two per cent, rising to six per cent by year nine.
body: The Alberta government on Friday, Nov. 13, proposed a voluntary 10-year royalty incentive for new oilsands developments and expansions, called the Oil Sands Growth Program [1]. Premier Danielle Smith and Energy and Minerals Minister Brian Jean announced it at a news conference with Finance Minister Jason Nixon and industry representatives [1].

Under the design Jean described, companies would apply for the program, and projects would need approval [1]. It would be open to new greenfield projects and to brownfield expansions that meet a production threshold of 5,000 barrels per day [1].

Approved projects would pay a royalty of two per cent in years one to five, three per cent in year six, four per cent in year seven, five per cent in year eight and six per cent in years nine and 10 [1]. If the regular oilsands royalty rate is lower during that time, the lower rate would apply, and projects would return to regular royalties after 10 years [1].
The province expects to launch the program in early 2027, subject to program and regulatory requirements, and wants companies to start construction before the end of 2029 [1].

Smith said the province is aiming for about eight million barrels of oil per day by 2035 [1]. She said resource revenues have recently brought in about $20 billion a year, just over a quarter of the provincial budget [1]. "Investors have choices about where they put that money," Smith said [1].

The remarks did not include modelling or an estimate of what the incentive would cost the province in royalties, according to EnergyNow's report [1]. Kendall Dilling, president of the Oil Sands Alliance, estimated that more than $100 billion in upstream investment would be needed to fill proposed pipeline additions and expansions [1].

Executives from Cenovus, Suncor, Canadian Natural Resources, ConocoPhillips Canada, Strathcona Resources and Imperial were acknowledged at the announcement, and the Explorers and Producers Association of Canada also spoke [1].

articles.title: Proposed city budget's fine print: higher fees, a bigger workforce and a costlier 2029 election
articles.dek: Details in the City of Calgary's proposed 2027-2030 budget include what each point of tax increase is worth and what it would take to trim next year's hike.
body: Documents behind the City of Calgary's proposed 2027-2030 budget contain a range of smaller items that council will weigh alongside the headline property tax increase, according to a review by LiveWire Calgary published Nov. 12 [1].

Each $25.6 million in spending equals one per cent on a typical single-family property tax bill [1]. Cutting five percentage points from the proposed 2027 increase would therefore take about $128 million in cuts or other measures, such as drawing on the Fiscal Stability Reserve [1]. Assessed values for all property types fell in 2026, so the city proposes raising the mill rate [1].

The city's workforce would grow from 19,411 to 22,946 positions by 2030, about 18 per cent [1]. The plan includes a new 11-person cyber security unit costing about $2.2 million a year, and councillors' office budgets would rise by $1.4 million a year from 2027, roughly $100,000 per ward [1].

The Calgary Police Commission's budget, unchanged at $1.39 million for eight years, would rise to $3.19 million [1]. The $28 million revenue loss from photo radar is funded for 2028 to 2030 but not for 2027 [1].

For transit riders, extending the transfer window from 90 to 120 minutes would cost $2 million a year [1]. Calgary Transit Access, the specialized transit service, needs another $1.4 million a year because contractor rates rose 25 per cent while funding covers 19.5 per cent, and some trips may be turned away [1].

Some fees would rise. One-day park programs would go from $270 to $395 and one-hour programs from $108 to $130, and a wedding at Devonian Gardens would rise about 13 per cent in 2027 [1]. A further $200,000 one-time grant would keep Inglewood Pool open until the MNP expansion is finished in the second quarter of 2027; without it, the pool would close at the end of 2026 [1].

The City Clerk is asking for $23.9 million for the 2029 municipal election, including $22.2 million for the election itself [1]. The 2025 election cost about $16 million and the 2021 election $8.5 million [1].

A zero-based review of city spending is not fully funded and may not begin until 2031 [1]. Council's budget deliberations are still ahead, and all of these figures are proposals that council can change [1].

articles.dek: Calgarians used 477 million litres on Thursday, and the City is also repairing a water main leak in Edgemont that may lower pressure in five northwest communities.
body: Calgary used 477 million litres of water on Thursday, Nov. 12, keeping the city below its 500-million-litre daily target while Stage 4 restrictions remain in place, the City and CTV News reported Friday [1][2].

The City says keeping use under that line matters while the new Bearspaw South Feeder Main is connected, because the city is mainly relying on one water treatment plant [1]. Global News reported earlier this week that the Bearspaw plant normally supplies about 20 per cent of daily needs and the Glenmore plant the other 80 per cent [3].

What has changed since Thursday's update is the pace of work. Starting the evening of Sunday, Nov. 15, crews will work 24 hours a day for about two weeks at 33 Avenue and 89 Street N.W., where they are cutting into the pipe to install a new valve [1]. At the Shaganappi Pump Station, new pipe sections are in place and welding has begun, and asphalt removal started Friday at 83 Street N.W. [1]. Drivers face single-lane alternating traffic and pedestrian detours at 83 Street N.W. and 33 Avenue N.W., and westbound turns onto 33 Avenue N.W. from 83 Street N.W. are not allowed [1].

Separately, the City began repairing a water main leak in Edgemont on Friday, a job expected to take about seven to 10 days [1]. Customers in Edgemont, Hamptons, Citadel, Hawkwood and Arbour Lake may notice lower water pressure, but the City says the water remains safe to drink [1]. Westbound Edgemont Drive N.W. is closed at Edgemont Boulevard N.W. [1].

As of Global's Nov. 9 report, restrictions were expected to stay in place for at least another three and a half weeks, and water chief operating officer Michael Thompson said the new pipe was expected to be in use by mid-December [3]. The City's latest update did not give a new end date [1].

articles.title: Calgary police suspend Crime Stoppers partnership during federal privacy investigation
articles.dek: The move reverses the service's position from late October, when it said it would keep accepting tips through the program after a data breach at the tip platform's vendor.
body: The Calgary Police Service is suspending its partnership with Crime Stoppers while the federal privacy commissioner investigates a data breach, CTV News reported on Thursday, Nov. 12 [1][2].

The breach happened earlier in 2026 [1]. According to Global News, the U.S.-based company Navigate360 manages the platform Crime Stoppers uses to receive tips, and the company said a third party accessed one of its systems and copied data between Nov. 21, 2025, and March 5, 2026 [3]. Names, addresses and other sensitive information may have been affected, though the company said it found no evidence the information had been used for fraud or identity theft [3]. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada is investigating the company's safeguards [3].

The suspension is a change for Calgary. In an Oct. 30 report, Global News said a Calgary police spokesperson had confirmed by email that the service was continuing to accept tips through Crime Stoppers, and that police were satisfied with added security measures after talking with Crime Stoppers Canada [3]. Several other police services in Canada had already suspended their use of the program by then [3].

The scale of the breach has been measured elsewhere. In Toronto, 176,859 tips submitted between January 2022 and November 2025 were affected, including 12,392 that may contain personal information, according to the chair of Toronto Crime Stoppers [3].

The reports read did not say when the Calgary suspension will end or what the police service is asking tipsters to do in the meantime [1][2]. In earlier coverage of other suspensions, Global News noted that people can still report information through regular police channels, which are not anonymous, and should call 911 in an emergency [3]. People worried about their personal information were advised to contact Crime Stoppers directly [3].

articles.title: Grey Cup Sunday brings road closures around McMahon Stadium; mild, partly cloudy weekend forecast
articles.dek: University Drive N.W. will close and Crowchild Trail will narrow from about 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. Sunday as Montreal and Edmonton meet in the 113th Grey Cup.
body: Drivers in northwest Calgary should expect closures and detours on Sunday, Nov. 15, when the Montreal Alouettes and Edmonton Elks play the 113th Grey Cup at McMahon Stadium [1]. Kickoff is at 5 p.m. and stadium gates open at 3 p.m. [1].

According to the City of Calgary details reported by Daily Hive, restrictions will be in place from about 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. [1]. University Drive N.W. will be fully closed between 16 Avenue and 24 Avenue N.W., with access limited to identified taxis, rideshare vehicles and vehicles with Grey Cup accreditation; residents can reach their homes through checkpoints by showing proof of address [1].

Crowchild Trail N.W. will be reduced to two lanes in each direction between 16 Avenue and 24 Avenue, with the speed limit lowered to 50 km/h and no left turns into the stadium area [1]. 23 Avenue N.W. will be closed between Crowchild Trail and Banff Trail N.W., and about 200 metres of Banff Trail N.W. will close near the Banff Trail CTrain station [1]. 24 Street N.W. becomes one-way northbound with a pickup and drop-off lane, and the public post-game pickup area is on 24 Street across Crowchild Trail, reached by the pedestrian overpass [1]. Temporary parking restrictions may apply in nearby neighbourhoods [1].
The City is encouraging fans to take Calgary Transit; Banff Trail station on the Red Line serves the stadium [1].

The weather should cooperate. CTV News forecasts a partly cloudy weekend with highs of 12 C to 14 C [2]. Grey Cup week festivities began in earnest on Thursday, when Calgary Grey Cup Committee chair Steve Sommerfeld rode a horse into a hotel lobby to kick off an annual tradition as fans arrived from across the country [3].

The game is the sixth Grey Cup held at McMahon, a 66-year-old stadium on University of Calgary land [4]. No decision has been made on a replacement; the City is running an early-stage feasibility study on major sports and event facilities [4]. Steve Allan, chair of the McMahon Stadium Society, told The Canadian Press, "It's time for a new building" [4].
